- **Magic-link relay and prefetch (item 14).** A link and a code are bound to the browser that
  asked, by a host-only `__Host-pkey_signin` cookie naming the flow; the link's token is 192 bits
  and only its peppered hash is a store key. Opening the link (`GET`) consumes nothing, so a mail
  scanner cannot burn it; its button `POST`s. Opened on another device it shows "Confirm sign-in,
  requested at <time> from <place>" and confirming only lets the asking browser finish: a link
  phished out of a victim signs in the attacker's own flow at most, never the device that opened
  it. A code and the link complete one flow once (atomic consume).
- **The flow outlives its code (PX-12).** The expired-link page offers **Send a new code** to the
  masked address, so the flow record and its `__Host-pkey_signin` cookie live one hour (the
  per-recipient send window) while the code and link keep their ten minutes. Nothing a ten-minute
  flow refused is allowed now: verify, the poll and the link's confirm check the code's age first
  (a stale code is `signin_expired`, no attempt counted), and the link record and the code still
  expire at ten minutes. What lives longer is the sealed address in the flow record and the right
  to ask this browser's own flow for a new code, under the resend's wait, the per-flow cap of 5 and
  I-02's limits. `GET /api/signin/flow` and the expired page show the address masked
  (`a•••@example.com`) and only to the browser holding the cookie; a link opened anywhere else, or
  one already used (its flow is gone), names no address. The page's form is a `POST` of the resend
  route. `SameSite=Lax` is scoped to the site, not the origin, so a sibling host on the same site
  could carry the cookie: the form `POST` is refused unless `Sec-Fetch-Site` is `same-origin` (or,
  without fetch metadata, `Origin` equals the request's), and a refusal is the missing-flow page
  (Sign in again), so no live code is retired and nothing is named.
- **The email gate and the join offer (owner decisions, 2026-10-04).** No account row and no
  session exist until the gate passes; its record is server-held and named by a host-only
  `__Host-pkey_gate` cookie, so another browser cannot drive it. A provider-asserted verified
  address (Apple's; Google's only for a Gmail address or a matching Workspace `hd`, PX-W15 below)
  is trusted as the provider's statement, which is the same trust I-06 places in that provider's
  ID token; anything else needs our code. An address
  another account uses stops the gate with an offer and writes nothing. Joining needs both
  identities proven in the one session: the gate proves the provider identity, and the other
  account is proven by a fresh (5-minute) account session in this browser or by the gate's code
  only when the address is an active email sign-in method of that account (a code to an address
  that is merely another account's primary email proves nothing). Linking and merging then run
  I-05's `linkIdentity` and `mergeAccounts`, with their own freshness checks and notices. Account
  creation is one atomic batch on the links' UNIQUE key, so a race leaves nothing behind.
- **Sessions (item 7).** The account cookie stays signed (realm-tagged) and also names a
  server-side `account_sessions` row by a random id whose peppered hash is the key; a revoked,
  expired or missing row refuses the cookie, so sign-out (server-side too), ending one session
  and "sign out everywhere" are real, and a table dump is not a set of cookies. All three account
  cookies are host-only on key.plrs.im (`__Host-`, `Path=/`), `HttpOnly`, `Secure`,
  `SameSite=Lax`. Because a host-only cookie still reaches every path on the host, the dispatcher
  removes the account realm's cookies from every product route's request and drops any
  `Set-Cookie` for them from its response (a test plants and reads through a product route), so
  product code can neither read nor plant the account session.
- **Profile import and avatars.** Provider names and locales are untrusted display data: names
  lose control, bidirectional and zero-width characters and are cut to 64 characters, locales
  must look like BCP 47, nothing is rendered as markup. Pictures: see "Account pictures (PX-W16)"
  below, which replaced I-07's own fetcher and its stored-as-fetched residual.

### Login-card providers: Google, Apple and Steam (I-06)

The login card signs people in with Google, Apple and Steam through Polaris's own platform
clients (S-16 §5.2): one Google OAuth client, one Apple Services ID and one Steam Web API key per
environment, under `/login/<provider>` (`services/identity/providers/`). They are account sign-in
methods, never behind a product's Identity toggle. S-16 §5.4 item 2 (broker confusion) is I-06's.

- **Broker confusion and audience (item 2).** `verifyProviderIdToken` takes the audience as a
  required argument and refuses an empty one, so there is no "any audience" mode: a login-card
  token must name exactly the platform client id (Google) or the Polaris Services ID (Apple), a
  multi-audience token must carry that client as `azp`, and a present `azp` must equal it. A token
  Apple or Google minted for a developer's bundle id (I-13's native sign-in) is therefore refused
  on the card. The exchange checks against the product's own audiences and `azp`, so a card token
  is refused there too (see "Platform sign-in (I-13)"). A provider is
  offered only when all of its values are set and its sealed secret opens, so a missing client id
  never reaches audience checking. Steam (OpenID 2.0) has no audience; its equivalents are an
  exact `openid.return_to` (our origin, our path and this flow's `state`) among the signed fields,
  `op_endpoint` = Steam's, and Steam's own `check_authentication` verdict, never the redirect's
  parameters alone. Every `openid.*` key (and `state`) must appear exactly once and the body sent
  to `check_authentication` is rebuilt from those single values, so a repeated `claimed_id` placed
  before Steam's genuine one cannot make the local checks and Steam's verdict look at two
  different identities (an account-takeover shape found in review).
- **Mix-up (RFC 9207).** Each provider has its own callback path and a flow records the provider
  it was started for; a `state` is never redeemed on another provider's callback. Where the
  provider advertises `authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported` (Google), `iss` is required
  on the authorization response, and a present `iss` must equal the issuer in any case.
- **Discovery is data (SSRF).** The discovery document is fetched from the provider's fixed
  issuer, its `issuer` must match exactly, and every URL it names (authorize, token, JWKS), like
  every other outbound provider call, passes one door (`providers/net.ts`): `https:` only, no
  credentials, the default port, no private, loopback or link-local literal, and a per-provider
  host allowlist. Redirects are never followed and bodies are capped at 64 KB, so a poisoned
  document cannot aim the token POST (which carries the client secret) or the key fetch elsewhere.
- **Login CSRF without a Lax cookie.** Apple answers with a cross-site `form_post`, on which a
  `SameSite=Lax` cookie is not sent, so the flow is found by its `state` alone, server-side, in
  the single-use store (peppered hash, ten minutes, consumed atomically by the first callback,
  burned by a cancel or failure). It is still bound to the browser that started it: start sets
  `__Host-pkey_signin` (random, `SameSite=None; Secure; HttpOnly`, ten minutes), whose hash the
  flow holds, and a callback without the matching cookie is refused. The cookie opens nothing by
  itself. Residual: a browser that blocks `SameSite=None` cookies on a cross-site top-level POST
  cannot finish Apple sign-in and is told to start again.
- **Credential custody.** The Google client secret, the Apple `.p8` and the Steam Web API key are
  Worker secrets holding `keyvault.seal` blobs bound to `pkey:v2:_platform:signin-provider-secret:<id>`,
  a slot no product slug can spell under a kind of its own; a copy of the Worker secret without
  the KEK is inert. The `.p8` only ever leaves as a five-minute ES256 client secret.
- **Upstream tokens.** ID tokens are verified once (signature against the provider JWKS, issuer,
  audience, `azp`, `nonce`, `iat` within the ID-token age) and never stored; the access and refresh
  tokens a token endpoint also returns are dropped unread. Apple's first-consent `user` field is
  unsigned, so it is only a display suggestion; the email always comes from the signed token.
- **Verified email.** `emailVerified` is true only when the provider asserted it in the signed
  token (`email_verified` `true`, or Apple's `"true"`); Steam supplies no email. The card never
  joins by email match (I-05); I-07's interstitial decides what an unverified or absent email needs.
- **Apple server-to-server notifications.** `POST /login/apple/notifications` accepts only a JWT
  signed by Apple, issued by Apple, addressed to the Services ID and at most seven days old (Apple
  retries). Events flag the link (`account_links.provider_flag`: `consent_revoked`,
  `account_deleted`, `email_disabled`) and are audited; they never delete it, since removing a
  method stays the person's own step-up action with its last-method guard. A replayed event only
  re-applies an idempotent flag. `account_deleted` is final; a fresh Apple sign-in clears
  `consent_revoked`, and `email-enabled` clears `email_disabled`.
- **Abuse.** Start, callback and notifications are rate limited per caller IP in their own
  buckets (`portalProviderStart`, `portalProviderCallback`, `appleNotifications`), all failing
  closed.

### The email gate: G31's checks and terms acceptances (PX-W15)

PORTAL.md §10.2 G31 on top of I-07's gate (`services/identity/card/gate.ts`, the "Login card"
section above): the provider rule checked end to end through I-06's callbacks, nothing issued
before the gate passes, and terms acceptances kept per account, product and version
(`account_terms_acceptances`, `accounts/terms.ts`).

- **Unverified provider emails.** Only a provider's signed assertion skips our code, and only
  where it vouches for the address today (`providerVouchesForEmail`): Apple's (always sent, a
  private-relay address included), and Google's `email_verified: true` only for `@gmail.com` /
  `@googlemail.com` or when the signed `hd` claim equals the address's domain (a Workspace
  account, whose addresses the domain's admin controls). A Google address with
  `email_verified: false` or outside that rule, every typed address and every Steam sign-in (no
  email at all) get a 6-digit code on I-02's store, bound to this gate's record (`flowId`), so a
  code sent for one gate cannot pass another. The rule is applied to the identity as it enters the
  gate, so the provider link stores such an address as unverified too: an address our code proved
  is verified on the email method only (tests).
- **Apple relay addresses.** A `…@privaterelay.appleid.com` address is accepted as Apple verified
  it and can be the account's primary email. It reaches the person only through Apple's relay,
  which accepts mail only from registered senders (`EMAIL_APPLE_RELAY`, I-02 above), and it does
  not match a purchase made with the person's real address; the step marks it (`relay: true`) and
  offers "Use my real email", which then needs a code (test).
- **Takeover through a claimed email.** The confirmed address becomes a verified account email,
  and verified emails attach unclaimed email-bound licences (`syncAccountLicenseLinks`). The gate
  therefore never accepts an address on anyone's word but the provider's signed token or our code,
  never creates a second account for an address another account uses, and answers `email_in_use`
  only after the address was proven, so the gate cannot be used to test addresses. Joining needs
  proof of the other account in the same browser (I-07). Closed (lead decision under the owner's
  delegation, 2026-10-06): Google's `email_verified` for an address outside Google's own domains
  says only that Google verified it once, not that the person still controls it (a former
  employee's company address). Such an address now needs our code unless the token's `hd` claim
  names its domain, and the Google link never stores it as verified, so it cannot claim licences
  bought with it (tests: Gmail and matching `hd` pass without a code; no `hd` and a mismatched
  `hd` get one).
- **Nothing before the pass.** The gate cookie (`__Host-pkey_gate`) authenticates nothing: until
  the pass no session cookie is set, no `account_sessions` row exists, no account row exists for
  a new identity, and every session-gated route (the account, its sessions, app consent for a
  passthrough request, device approval) answers 401 to that browser, at every step: opened, terms
  refused, code out, wrong code, join offer and refused join, and a terms-only gate on an existing
  account (tests). The pass is the one response that sets the session cookie and hands back the
  passthrough `request`, so no app token can be minted against an account whose gate is open.
- **Terms acceptances.** One row per (account, product, version), written once: a repeat
  acceptance keeps the first time and URL, and a new version adds a row beside the earlier ones,
  so the record of what the person agreed to survives the next version. The gate asks again while
  the current version has no row, and an old version never passes a gate opened for a new one.
  A merge moves the absorbed account's rows to the survivor (the survivor's own row stands for a
  version both accepted); account deletion and product deletion erase them (tests).

### Passkeys on key.plrs.im (I-16)

Passkeys are an account sign-in method on the console host (`services/identity/passkeys/`, over
`@simplewebauthn/server`; S-16 §5.4 items 7, 14 and 17; PORTAL.md §4.1, §4.26). Each passkey is
an `account_passkeys` row (COSE public key, signature counter, transports, RP id, user handle)
twinned with an `account_links` row (`issuer_key = 'passkey'`, subject = the credential id), so
the link engine's rules (one account per method, the never-orphan guard, step-up, audit, notices,
merge and deletion) apply to it unchanged.

- **Phishing and look-alike origins (item 14).** The relying party is the console host
  (`CONSOLE_ORIGIN`, `key.plrs.im`), and a ceremony is served only on that origin, so no other host
  of ours can mint a challenge a key.plrs.im passkey would answer. Both verifications pin the exact
  origin (`https://key.plrs.im`: no subdomain, no `http:`, no port) and the SHA-256 of the RP id in
  the authenticator data, so an assertion a browser makes for a look-alike site is refused here
  (tests for a sibling subdomain, the parent domain, `http:` and a foreign RP id). The browser
  itself refuses to use a key.plrs.im passkey anywhere else, which is the phishing resistance;
  the server checks make it independent of the browser.
- **Replay (item 8's single-use rule).** A sign-in challenge is 32 random bytes in I-02's
  single-use store for 5 minutes, named by a host-only `__Host-pkey_passkey` cookie (so it
  completes only in the browser that asked) and TAKEN by an atomic consume before anything is
  verified: an answer verifies at most once, a failed try needs a new challenge, and of two racing
  submissions of one answer exactly one signs in (the workerd test races them on the real Durable
  Object). An old answer to a new challenge fails the challenge comparison. A registration
  challenge is bound to the account session that asked, consumed the same way. The account realm's
  cookie rules cover the new cookie: the dispatcher strips it from every product route.
- **What the assertion must prove.** User presence AND user verification (biometric or device
  PIN) at registration and sign-in: a passkey is a whole sign-in, never a second factor. The user
  handle must come back and equal the one the credential was created under (a discoverable sign-in
  names no account up front). The signature must verify under the stored key. Algorithms: EdDSA,
  ES256, RS256. No attestation is requested; a statement an authenticator sends anyway is still
  verified. A passkey signs in only through its existing link (`signIn` with `linkedOnly`), so it
  never creates an account, even in the instant after its method was removed.
- **Cloned authenticators.** A signature counter that did not advance while either side is
  non-zero refuses the sign-in (WebAuthn §7.2 step 22) and writes `account.passkey.counter_regressed`
  to the account's audit trail. The library compares counters BEFORE it checks the signature, so
  it is handed 0 and the same rule runs on the counter of an assertion whose signature is proven:
  a forgery cannot plant a false clone alarm (a test). The counter update is a compare-and-set,
  so of two assertions racing on one counter value at most one is accepted. Synced passkeys
  report 0 and are unaffected; cloning them is the sync provider's account security.
- **Enrolment and the account as a target (item 17; S-16 §5.1 recovery).** A passkey is added only
  once the account has a verified primary email (so it is never the only way back in), only with
  a sign-in no older than 5 minutes (re-checked when the answer arrives), is audited
  (`account.link.add`) and emailed to every verified address, and an account holds at most 20.
  Removal needs the same step-up and goes through `unlinkIdentity`, whose guard is inside the
  DELETE, so the last sign-in method is never removed (`last_link`); the generic unlink also
  deletes the passkey's WebAuthn material. A credential id is stored with a plain INSERT in one
  batch with its link: an authenticator can choose its own ids, so a credential id another account
  holds fails the batch (`link_conflict`) and can never overwrite that account's key.
- **Correlation.** The WebAuthn user handle is 32 random bytes per account
  (`accounts.passkey_user_handle`), never the account id and derived from nothing; the user name
  the authenticator shows is the person's own primary email. One handle per account means one
  "Polaris Key" entry per authenticator. Nothing about passkeys reaches a developer: they are
  account methods, and a passkey sign-in on the card is the platform's, never a product's.
- **Enumeration.** The sign-in challenge names no account (no credential list). Every failed
  verification (unknown credential, wrong RP id or user handle, a bad signature, origin,
  challenge or flags, a counter that did not advance) answers one `401 unauthorized` body;
  `unknownCredential: true` says only that no account holds that credential id (so the card can
  ask the browser to forget it), which reveals nothing about any account. A malformed request
  (`400 bad_request`) or a missing, used or expired challenge (`400 signin_expired`) is refused
  before any passkey is looked up, so it says nothing about one. A disabled account answers
  `403 forbidden` only after the passkey's own signature verified, so only the holder of that
  passkey learns it. Both card routes share 30 requests a minute per client address and fail
  closed; account changes are limited to 10 a minute per account.
- **Rename (PX-W19).** `PATCH /api/me/passkeys/<id>` sets a label only: owner-only (the account id
  is in the UPDATE, and an unknown id and another account's answer the same 404), step-up, 1 to 64
  characters with no control or bidirectional characters, body read under a 1 KiB cap. The name is
  never read by verification, never put in an email or audit summary, and is shown to its owner as
  text (the console renders it escaped).
- **Residuals.** Whoever holds an unlocked device with a synced passkey, or the sync account
  behind it, can sign in as the person: that is the authenticator's security, as for any passkey
  site. Pocket ID passkeys (`rp_id = id.plrs.im`) cannot carry over; migrated users enrol again
  (I-17). AAGUIDs are stored for display only and are not verified (no attestation); a malicious
  authenticator can claim any model, which affects only the label the person sees.

### Sign-in methods and joining accounts (PX-W12)

Account → Sign-in methods and Link an existing account (`services/identity/portal/methods.ts`,
`portal/link.ts`, `accounts/mergeUndo.ts`; PORTAL.md §4.11, §4.26, §10.2 G27) put I-05's link
engine and merge behind portal routes. S-16 §5.4 item 3 (account takeover through linking) and
item 15 (merge takeover) are the threats; the rules below are what the routes add.

- **Connect.** Every connect needs a sign-in no older than 5 minutes, re-checked when the change
  lands (`linkIdentity`), so a stolen days-old cookie cannot add an attacker's method as a way back
  in. A provider connect reuses the provider's registered sign-in callback, the single-use flow
  record and the `SameSite=None` binding cookie (so a callback finishes only in the browser that
  started it), and the record carries the account and its session row because Apple's form_post
  sends no Lax session cookie; the callback refuses when that session was signed out or revoked
  meanwhile, and it never signs anyone in or opens the email gate. The provider's email claim is
  narrowed exactly as at sign-in (`providerVouchesForEmail`), and an address another account uses
  is stored unverified, so a connect cannot make one address verified on two accounts (which would
  hand that address's waiting licences to the wrong account). An email connect sends a code bound
  to the session that asked, under I-02's send and attempt limits, and answers its start
  identically whatever the address; whose the address is shows only after the code proved it. A
  method another account holds is refused (`link_conflict`) and nothing moves.
- **Disconnect.** The same step-up; the last method is never removed (`last_link`, guarded inside
  the DELETE, so two racing removals cannot orphan the account, a test); the only address cannot
  go while it is the primary, so notices and passkey enrolment always have a verified address
  (guarded in the same DELETE, with the promotion of the next address in the same batch, a test).
  Every change is audited and emailed to every verified address; an email method is named
  generically in those notices, so no notice hands one of the account's addresses to the others,
  and a removed address is told too.
- **Join with proof of both, in one browser.** Linking starts from a fresh session and records its
  proof in a server-held flow named by a host-only `__Host-pkey_link` cookie (15 minutes; the
  dispatcher strips it from product routes like every account-realm cookie, and signing out
  clears it). The second proof is only ever the session presenting that cookie, after a real
  sign-in (the login card, or a PX-W14 device approval, which also mints a fresh session), so both
  proofs come from one browser and neither can be supplied by another party's session (a test).
  The merge refuses unless both proofs are under 5 minutes old, the link routes also refuse when
  either proof's session was signed out, and the join screen shows an account's details only
  while its proof's session is live. The flow is claimed before the merge, so two racing confirms
  merge once (a test). Nothing looks at email addresses: never by email match.
- **Undo for 72 hours.** Every join (the login card's offer too) records a snapshot of what moved
  in `account_merges`, in the merge's own batch. The kept account can undo with a fresh sign-in,
  which a person whose method was joined away can always get (their methods sign in to the kept
  account), so a join made with stolen proof of one account is reversible by its owner after the
  notice. Only methods still on the kept account go back: a method disconnected since the join (a
  lost passkey, a compromised provider account) never comes back silently, and the snapshot holds
  method ids only, never their subjects, addresses or keys. Nor does an address come back as the
  restored account's primary email on the snapshot's word: a primary none of the returning
  methods carries (verified, if the primary is) gives way to the oldest verified address they
  carry, or to none (a test). The undo refuses (`last_link`) when an
  account would be left with no way to sign in; that guard is the first statement of the undo's
  batch and aborts it, so a removal racing the undo cannot orphan either side (a test). A licence
  that goes back revokes every registry token the kept account minted on it during the window
  (F-21, `onLicenseOwnershipEnded`) and every operator-minted token of it (F-33b.1, including ones
  minted before the join) and clears its devices' bindings; the absorbed account's own
  tokens move back untouched (a test). A join is refused while EITHER account could still undo a
  join of its own (`merge_pending`): absorbing that account would destroy its undo, and absorbing
  into it would hand the second join's data and aliases to the first join's absorbed account on
  undo. It is refused as well while either account has a scheduled deletion (`deletion_pending`,
  under account erasure below), and an undo leaves such a request with the account it was made
  for. The snapshot holds the absorbed person's details: it is cleared by the undo, deleted
  nightly once the window ends, and deleted with either account (docs/PRIVACY.md).
- **Make primary (PX-W19).** `POST /api/me/methods/<id>/primary` needs the same step-up as a
  connect, takes only one of the caller's own email methods (an unknown id and another account's
  answer the same 404; another kind is 422), and writes `primary_email` with one conditional
  statement that holds only while that link still belongs to the account, so a removal racing it
  cannot leave a primary with no method. Every email method exists only after its code or a
  provider's verified claim, so no unverified address becomes primary. A change is audited and a
  notice naming no address goes to every verified address, the old primary included. Products
  see the new address on their next read of the consent view and developers on the next
  product-user contact read; nothing is pushed to them.
- **Residuals.** Someone with a fresh session for an account can already change it directly
  (connect their own method, disconnect the others, delete it); joining gives them nothing more,
  and the notices to every verified address of both accounts are the detection. Deleting the kept
  account inside the window deletes the snapshot, so the joined account cannot be restored
  afterwards (the deletion is itself step-up gated and emailed). An undo does not split account ×
  product data a store already re-keyed (`runSubjectMerge`), and developers keep the
  `subject.merged` alias they were told about; the restored account gets a fresh pairwise subject
  where its old one became an alias, so to that developer it is a new person, and no
  `subject.unmerged` event exists (`subject_events` allows only merged and deleted). A device
  activated during the window on one of the absorbed account's licences keeps its seat; its
  binding to the kept account's subject is cleared with the licence's other bindings at the undo,
  but a device bound to the kept account's subject on a licence that stays with the kept account
  is untouched. A picture the kept account did not use may be swept before an undo
  (`sweepAvatars`, after a day), and the restored account then shows initials. A kept account
  that took the joined account's WebAuthn user handle and created a passkey under it during the
  window keeps that handle after an undo, so both accounts share one `passkey_user_handle`.
  Availability only: a credential is found by its id and belongs to one account, so neither signs
  in as the other, but an authenticator keeps one passkey per RP id and user handle, and enrolling
  on one account can replace the other's, which then signs in another way.

### The console's Users page and the relink tool (I-12)

Every product's console has a Users page (`/manage/api/products/<slug>/users…`,
`console/handlers/users.ts`, queries in `services/identity/accounts/productUsers.ts`). It is Core,
not Identity: the account is platform-level, so a product with Identity off lists its licence
owners too. S-16 §5.4 items 9 (no recovery desk: the developer's relink is the recovery path)
and 12 (cross-tenant correlation) are the deltas.

- **Cross-tenant correlation (item 12).** A row is keyed by this product's pairwise subject, and
  every query carries the product. Every field a response carries is named in `productUsers.ts`;
  none is the account id, a link, or another product's licence, session or datum (tests read
  every route for product A and B of one account and find neither the account id nor B's
  subject, licence or data). Search matches a subject prefix, an exact licence id or a buyer
  email prefix, never the account's primary email, so the page is not an "is this person a
  Polaris Key user" oracle. The account email is shown only with the person's consent for this
  product (`account_product_grants.claims_json` holds `email`; D19). A subject minted only for a
  support code stays unlisted until it holds a licence, a signed-in device or a sign-in. A
  search by support code finds it, within the product.
- **Readable support codes (I-41).** The code a person reads out is not the subject: nine
  characters from a 30-symbol alphabet without lookalikes (`core/accounts/supportCodes.ts`,
  `support_codes`, one stable code per (product, person)). It is an identifier for that
  product's support, never a credential: it opens no session, licence, key or data, and the
  signed licence and the export still carry the subject. Three rows:
  - _Enumeration._ 30^8 (about 6.6e11) codes: eight symbols drawn by rejection sampling and a ninth
    that is their Luhn mod 30 check, so a guess hits a real code with probability under 2e-6 per
    try even with a million codes issued, and a wrong symbol is refused as a check failure before
    any lookup (public math, no oracle). The console
    route `GET /manage/api/support-codes/<code>` is rate-limited per operator (30 a minute,
    `adminSupportCode`) on top of the admin API budget, and answers only an operator who may read
    the product, so a guess is also a sign-in away. Guessing finds a product's own customer
    only, and that customer's subject, which the Users page already shows that operator.
  - _Cross-tenant._ The route resolves a code to `{product, subject}` and then checks
    `can(product, core, view)`. A code of another product, an unknown code, a malformed one and
    an operator without the area all answer the same `404` (`test/surfaces/console/supportCodes.test.ts`), so it
    is no oracle for another tenant's customers. The Users search is an exact lookup within the
    product in the URL; the relink target accepts a code of THIS product only.
  - _Code versus subject._ The portal never shows the subject, and a lookup never returns the
    account id or email. Erasure (`deletion.ts`) deletes the code with the subject; a merge
    leaves the absorbed subject's code resolving to the survivor, and the account being merged
    away leaks nothing new because both are the same person to that product.
- **Relink (item 9).** The target is named only by a subject of THIS product (`target_not_found`
  otherwise; never an email, never another product's subject). The operator needs an interactive
  sign-in no older than 5 minutes (`session.stepUpAt`, set only by a `stepUp=1` flow whose ID token
  carries `auth_time`, which an ordinary sign-in never sets; `isSteppedUp`); `/manage/login?stepUp=1` shows the
  card first, and only its Continue (`go=1`) starts the flow, which sends `prompt=login` and `max_age=0`;
  the callback refuses a step-up whose `auth_time` is already
  stale. A reason (1 to 500 characters) is mandatory. Both accounts are emailed at their verified
  addresses BEFORE the owner pointer moves; the move is a conditional reassign (a concurrent change
  answers `conflict` and nothing is recorded), it is audited with before and after, and the
  `license_relinks` row (0072) keeps the reason, the actor and a 72-hour undo. The undo needs the
  same step-up and a reason, and works only while the licence still sits on the target account (a
  later relink, a detach or a deletion closes it). More than `RELINK_DAILY_ALERT_COUNT` (5) relinks
  by one operator in 24 hours raises `identity.relink.alert` in the platform audit trail. An
  account deletion clears the relink row's account ids, so an undo then leaves the licence
  floating rather than resurrecting a deleted owner.
- **What a developer can never do.** Disable, sign out, merge or delete an account, or touch its
  links: no route exists. Per-subject data deletion runs the subject-store registry's deletes
  (config overrides, Cloud Sync) and leaves the subject, its licences and the account.
- **Residuals.** An IdP that ignores `prompt=login` AND sends no `auth_time` lets a silent SSO
  count as a fresh sign-in (the callback time stands in); the console's IdP client (I-03) should be
  configured to honour both. A
  developer who already holds a buyer email can still find that buyer's row by it: the email is
  the developer's own record. The step-up window is enforced server-side; the console's own check
  only decides whether to offer the form or "Sign in again".

### The console sign-in card (ST-30, slice 1)

**Threat.** `GET /manage/login` used to redirect straight to the IdP. It now serves a card, so the
page, its policy and the redirect it leads to are new surface: a sign-in that starts without a
click, a card policy that lets a form post anywhere, a 401 that tells an unauthenticated caller
about sessions, and an address typed into a URL.

**Controls and rows.**

- **The card starts no flow.** `GET /manage/login` answers 200 with a script-free page and sets no
  cookie and writes no flow record. Only `go=1` (the Continue button) starts PKCE, sets the
  binding cookie and counts against the `adminLogin` limit (20 a minute per network); viewing the
  card is not counted, so a refresh cannot lock anyone out. `returnTo` is re-checked by
  `sanitizeReturnTo` before it is written into the page or the flow.
- **`form-action` names the IdP.** Browsers apply `form-action` to every redirect a submission
  follows, so the card's policy is `form-action 'self'` plus the configured issuer's origin and the
  authorization-endpoint origin from discovery, never an origin from the request. `discover()`
  validates the endpoint before it is used: https only, no port, no credentials, no reserved or
  private address, and a host on the issuer's allowlist. A failed discovery adds nothing; the
  card then shows and Continue answers the 502 card. The origin set is cached with discovery and a
  failed discovery is remembered briefly (45 s) for card views, so an IdP outage does not turn every
  view into an outbound fetch.
- **The expired-session marker.** The console API's 401 carries `X-PKey-Session: expired` only when
  the request presented a console session cookie (and no bearer token) that does not resolve. A
  forged, expired and revoked cookie look the same, a request with no cookie gets no header, and
  the answer reveals nothing a caller without a cookie could not already see (it names no account
  and no reason). Same-origin only: the API sends no CORS headers, so a page on another origin
  cannot read it.
- **`login_hint`.** The typed address is passed to the IdP as `login_hint` only when it is a single
  plausible address of at most 254 characters; anything else is dropped. It is a hint: the IdP
  decides who signs in and the callback decides who may use the console, so a wrong or hostile
  hint changes nothing about access. It is not stored.
- **Use another account.** The 403 card's action goes straight to the IdP with
  `prompt=select_account`, or `prompt=login` when discovery does not list `select_account`. A
  step-up keeps `prompt=login` and `max_age=0` and ignores this parameter.
- **The 403 card names the account.** "{email} can't open this console" shows the address the IdP
  just verified for this browser, to that browser only, on a `no-store` page with
  `referrer-policy: no-referrer`; it adds nothing a person who just typed it does not know. The
  email is HTML-escaped.
- **The step-up email comes from the verified session.** The card shows and forwards an address
  only from `sessionFromRequest` (signature, expiry and revocation checked), never from the query.
  Without a valid session the step-up card shows the ordinary field.
- **The address is in the body, not the URL (slice 2a).** The card's Continue is a `POST
/manage/login` answered with a 303 to the IdP (SIGN-IN.md §3.13), so the typed address never
  appears in a URL the browser visits on this origin (history, access logs). The POST is accepted
  only from this origin (`Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin`, else a same-origin `Origin`), as
  `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, under 4 KB; anything else is a 403 or 413 card. The start
  is counted against the same `adminLogin` limit as the `go=1` link. A cross-site page that POSTs
  here can start a flow only for the browser it posts from, which then has to complete it itself
  (the flow is bound to that browser's `__Host-pkey_admin_flow` cookie), so it gains nothing; the
  same-origin rule keeps the limit ours. The error pages whose retry is a POST (`502`) carry the
  same `form-action` as the card, because the browser applies THIS page's policy to the redirect
  their form follows. The `go=1` GET link remains for "Use another account" and the error
  actions, which carry no typed address; it still forwards a `login_hint` that is in its query.
  Residual: that link, if someone hand-builds it with a `login_hint`, shows the address in a URL
  they wrote themselves.
- **Help and Privacy under the card** are fixed same-host paths (`/docs/help/`,
  `/docs/help/your-data/`) written by the page, never taken from a request, on docs pages that
  need no session (`DOCS_TIERS` `public`). There is no Terms link: no Terms page exists yet.

Tests: `test/surfaces/console/brandPages.test.ts` (the card, its `form-action`, the error cards, no limit on
views), `test/surfaces/console/identityBinders.test.ts` (`login_hint`), `test/surfaces/admin.test.ts` (the 401 marker),
`packages/admin/e2e/consoleSignin.e2e.test.ts` (Continue reaches the IdP in Chromium under the real
policy).

### Console cookie v2, account sessions and the strong-method rule (ST-30, slices 2a and 2b)

**What arrived.** The console cookie carried the IdP's `sub` and `groups` for 8 h and could be
ended only by a per-operator mark or by rotating the secret. Nothing tied it to a Polaris Key
account, a disabled or deleted account kept its console session, and "which issuer may sign an
operator in" was implicit in one environment variable.

**Control.**

- **Cookie v2** (`core/console/session.ts`): signed under the tag `pkey.admin.v2|`, body `{aid, sid,
name, email, csrf, exp, authAt, stepUpAt?}` and no `groups` or `sub`. `aid` and `sid` only point;
  nothing in the cookie grants. A v1 body signed under the v1 tag cannot verify as v2 and the
  reverse (different signed message), so neither can be replayed as the other, and a cookie with
  edited fields fails its MAC. `test/surfaces/console/consoleSessionV2.test.ts` pins both.
- **The live check** (`console/consoleSession.ts`, `consoleSubject` in Identity): each request
  resolves `aid` + `sid` to a live `account_sessions` row (present, unrevoked, unexpired, held by
  `aid`), an active account that is still that account (a merge or deletion removed the row the
  cookie names), not on the erasure ledger, holding a link through the console IdP, and a sign-out
  mark that does not cover the session. The answer is remembered per session per isolate for
  `LIVE_CHECK_SECONDS` (30 s, `core/console/session.ts`, in the limits inventory), positive or
  negative. So "Sign out everywhere", a disabled or deleted account, a merge and a sign-out end
  console access within 30 s; sign-out also drops the row and this isolate's memory at once. A
  read that throws (database down) is neither remembered nor swallowed: the request fails, it does
  not grant. A v2 cookie presented where no database is passed (the docs gate before this change)
  is refused, never trusted.
- **v1 cookies keep working until they expire** (`sessionFromRequest`): the reader still accepts a
  v1 token (8 h at most) and checks the sign-out mark, so a deploy does not sign anyone out. The
  sign-in no longer mints v1 (`issueSession` stays as the v1 minter for tests). Delete the v1
  reader and `issueSession` once the last v1 cookie has expired.
- **One account per operator** (`consoleSignIn`, I-05 `signIn` through the portal's issuer key):
  the callback gates on the principal first, so an identity outside the platform-admin group gets
  no account and no cookie. An operator whose verified address another account already uses (a
  Polaris Locker account made with an email code) is joined to that account when exactly one
  ACTIVE account uses it (a disabled one is refused before anything is written) and the IdP vouched for the address (ST-28 SM-3(b)); anyone else, an unverified
  address, or an ambiguous address is refused with a card and writes nothing. The join writes an
  `account.link` row in the account's own history. Lead ruling (accepted): the join by IdP-verified email needs the platform-admin group, so the
  actor is already root, and allowlisted non-console IdPs cannot reach it. Also accepted: the live
  check's cache clears at 500 entries, and groups may be stale for up to 8 h as described below.
- **`operatorIssuerAllowed`** (`core/rbac/operatorIssuer.ts`) is the one place that decides which
  issuer may sign an operator in. The console IdP always qualifies; any other issuer only when its
  `https` host is on `OIDC_ISSUER_ALLOWLIST`, and it **fails closed**: unset or empty admits
  nothing else, in every environment (unlike `issuerHostAllowed`, which is fail-open outside
  prod because it guards a different sink). Both the sign-in and `consoleSubject` ask it, so a
  link through an issuer that stops qualifying stops yielding a subject within 30 s.
- **Groups are read from the console link** (`consoleSubject`), rewritten at each sign-in and
  never carried in the cookie. Slice 2b computes the root rule on top of them (below), so a stale
  assertion no longer roots anyone.
- **The account id stays off console bodies**: `/me` answers the member id (below), never the
  account id (`test/surfaces/console/consoleSessionV2.test.ts` asserts `/me` omits it).
- **"Open console" and "My library"** are pointers. The Locker account menu shows "Open console"
  only when `GET /api/me` answers a `console` address, which it does for an account whose console
  link's last-asserted groups carry the platform-admin group through an allowed issuer; the console
  decides on arrival. The console's "My library" link is the customer origin the console already
  knows (`/me.customerOrigin`).
- **"Your session ended" in place** (admin SPA): a 401 marked `X-PKey-Session: expired` with a page
  open shows a dialog and does not navigate. "Sign in again" is a plain link that opens the card in
  a second tab (`rel=noopener`), which lands on `/manage/#/signed-in` (a `returnTo` the existing
  allowlist already admits) and tells the first tab over a same-origin `BroadcastChannel`; the
  first tab then re-reads `/me`, which re-arms its CSRF token. The channel carries no secret and
  grants nothing: a page on another origin cannot join it, a script on this origin could already
  call the API.
  **A held write is replayed only as the account that started it.** The page records who `/me` said
  it was when the session ended. When the second tab signs in as someone else, every held request
  fails with its 401 (never sent under the new session's cookie or CSRF token), the page reloads its
  data as the new account, and a toast says "Signed in as <name>. Your unsaved change was not sent."
  A held request also fails, unreplayed, after 10 minutes (`HOLD_LIMIT_MS`). Tests:
  `packages/admin/test/sessionEnded.test.tsx`, and the different-account case in the Chromium e2e.

**Slice 2b: the strong-method rule, the computed root rule and the audit actor.**

- **SM-1, a strong method only** (`consoleSignIn`, `consoleSubject`; migration
  `0128_console_strong_method.sql` adds `account_links.strong_at`, `asserted_at` and `member_id`, all NULL on
  existing rows, and an index on `member_id`). The console is entered, and every 30 s check passes, only through a link that has
  `strong_at` set, through an issuer `operatorIssuerAllowed` still admits (SM-2, read at every use,
  never frozen into `strong_at`). An email code, a method added in the portal and a console-IdP link
  made by the portal path are never strong (SM-4). A sign-in whose link is known, is not strong and
  whose ID token does not assert the platform-admin group is refused with reason `method` **before
  anything is written** (no `signIn`, no touch, no session row); the card reads "That sign-in can't
  open this console / Use your company account or a passkey. An email code can't." The callback's
  own gate (a grant) runs first, so this refusal is the second line, and `consoleSubject` is the
  third: a session whose link loses `strong_at` is refused within 30 s.
- **SM-3, how a link becomes strong.** Only (b) a link the console-IdP sign-in itself created
  (a new account, or a join where the IdP vouched for the address and the actor holds the group)
  and (c) a console-IdP sign-in whose ID token asserts `PLATFORM_ADMIN_GROUP`, marked
  (`markLinkStrong`, first mark wins) before the strength check so today's operators get in at their
  next sign-in. SM-3(a) (a passkey enrolled after a console step-up) and (d) ("Use for the
  console") need the passkey button and are the next slice. No other code sets `strong_at`.
- **SM-5.** Removing a method needs no strong session; an account left with no strong link keeps
  its account and loses console entry (`consoleSubject` is null). A method added again later is
  weak until SM-3 runs.
- **The root rule is computed from the link at every check** (`rootRuleHolds`,
  `core/rbac/principal.ts`): strong, the platform-admin group in `groups_json`, and `asserted_at`
  within `ADMIN_SESSION_TTL_SECONDS` (8 h) of now (an `asserted_at` more than 60 s in the future is
  not fresh). Any missing value denies. `asserted_at` is written only in the same `UPDATE` as
  `groups_json` (`recordLinkGroups`, `recordLinkAssertion`), never by a sign-in that does not
  rewrite them, so it is not `last_used_at` and a path that skips the groups cannot extend a stale
  group. `consoleSubject` offers the stored groups only while that holds (else `[]` and
  `root: false`), and a v2 session's principal takes `root` from it; the 8 h bound still applies to
  a v1 cookie (its own expiry) and to a session kept open after the group was removed at the IdP.
  The groups gate at the callback still uses the groups the IdP asserted in that request.
- **The audit actor is the member id.** A v2 session's `sub` is `mbr_` + the first 22 base64url
  characters of `HMAC-SHA-256(memberKey, accountId)`, where `memberKey =
HMAC-SHA-256(KEY_HASH_PEPPER, "pkey/console-member-key/v1")` (`core/console/memberId.ts`): the
  pepper never keys the account id directly. It is the `actor_sub` of every console audit row, the
  limiter key and what `/me` answers, so the account id appears in none of them. With the pepper
  unset `memberKey` is `SHA-256(label)` (as every peppered hash falls back); rotating the pepper
  re-keys every id, the pepper's existing cost. Old rows keep the IdP `sub`, `actor_name` and
  `actor_email` and are never rewritten. The activity filter `actor=` accepts either id and
  `consoleActorAliases` expands it to both for the same person with indexed reads:
  `account_links.member_id` (written at each console sign-in, indexed) gives the account, the id is
  **recomputed from that account and must equal the filter** (a stale or planted column maps
  nothing), then the account's console-IdP subjects are read; an unknown value matches only itself.
  `/me.priorSubs` carries the IdP `sub` so the SPA still says "you" on old records. Sign-out writes
  the sign-out mark under the member id and the IdP `sub`; a v1 cookie's sign-out resolves the
  member id from its IdP subject and writes both, so it ends the operator's v2 sessions too.
- **v1 cookies and API tokens stay groups-only roots.** Until the last v1 cookie expires (at most
  8 h after the deploy) and for admin API tokens, a session's groups alone root it; the computed
  rule applies to v2 sessions only.
- **Merge, disable and delete end console eligibility on the link side.** A merge clears
  `strong_at` and `asserted_at` on the absorbed account's links in the same batch that moves them
  (the survivor does not inherit the operator's access; the person signs in through the console IdP
  once more; a merge undo restores the link but not the mark); the survivor's own links are
  untouched. Disabling flips the status, mirrors it, revokes the account's sessions and clears its links'
  strength in ONE batch (re-enabling does not bring a cookie back, and a crash cannot leave
  strength on a disabled account); starting an erasure clears them too (the commit deletes the links).
  The 30 s status check already ended the session; this makes the link side agree.
- **Tests:** `test/surfaces/console/consoleStrongMethod.test.ts` (each SM row allowed and refused, nothing written
  on a refusal, the root rule at each condition and at the 8 h edge, `asserted_at` moving only with
  the groups, the member id, the actor alias mapping over old and new rows, merge / disable /
  delete), `test/surfaces/console/consoleSessionV2.test.ts`.

**Residual.** The 30 s window is a deliberate cost: a revoked session can serve requests for up to
30 s in an isolate that cached it as live. The cache is per isolate, so a different isolate asks
D1 again. The v1 reader exists until its last cookie expires. A group removed at the IdP still ends root
only when the assertion ages out (8 h) for a session that is already open, because a refused
sign-in writes nothing. Not yet built: SM-3(a)/(d) (step-up enrolment), break-glass, the passkey
button, membership as bindings (ST-31). Residual of the migration: it holds three `ADD COLUMN`
statements and an index in one file (the lead may split it into `_a`/`_b` per R11-04); a replay fails at the
first statement and strands nothing.

Slice 2a tests: `test/surfaces/console/consoleSessionV2.test.ts` (sign-in lands on one account, cookie shape, the 30 s
check with a fake clock, disabled / deleted / merged / foreign-row / expired-row refusals, sign-out,
v1 compatibility, forged and cross-tagged tokens, `consoleSubject`, `operatorIssuerAllowed`'s unset /
empty / listed / unlisted / http cases, the Locker pointer), `test/surfaces/adminSessions.test.ts`,
`test/surfaces/console/brandPages.test.ts` (the POST, its refusals, the retry form), `packages/admin/test/sessionEnded.test.tsx`
(the overlay, axe), `packages/admin/e2e/consoleSignin.e2e.test.ts` and `consoleSessionEnded.e2e.test.ts`
(Chromium under the Worker's CSP).

### Console role bindings: the principal (ST-31.2)

**What arrived.** `console_role_bindings` (ST-31.1: `account_id` or `email_norm`, `role`, `scope`,
`areas_json`, `source`; `account_id` is `REFERENCES accounts(id) ON DELETE CASCADE`, so deleting or
merging an account removes its bindings) existed but nothing read it. The principal was the
root rule alone.

**Control.**

- **The principal is the root rule plus the stored bindings of the session's account**
  (`core/rbac/principal.ts`). `callerFor` (`console/api.ts`) passes `session.aid`; `resolvePrincipal`
  appends `listAccountGrants` after the root grant and drops exact duplicates. Roles still sum and
  there are no deny rules, so a binding can add reach and never remove the root rule's.
- **Per request, no cache.** The bindings are one indexed D1 read on each request, so a deleted
  binding stops granting on the next request. The only cached part is the 30 s live check of the
  session (`LIVE_CHECK_SECONDS`), which bounds a disabled account, a revoked session and a merge,
  all of which still answer 401 whatever the account's bindings. A cache on the bindings that
  outlived 30 s would be a trigger under ST-28 section 5.3 "New section 9 triggers" (listed in section 9).
- **`aid` points, it does not grant.** `aid` comes from a v2 cookie whose session row the live check
  resolved to this account (`row.account_id === cookie.aid`). A v1 cookie and a `pkeya_` token session
  carry none (`verifySession` now deletes `aid`, `sid` and `root` from a v1 body as well), so they stay
  root-only: a token never gains a stored grant. The sign-in gate in `console/auth.ts` still resolves
  the root rule alone and is unchanged, so until ST-31.8 no non-root person can mint a cookie.
- **Fail closed on a row it cannot read.** `rowToGrant` drops an unknown area (checked against
  `PRODUCT_AREAS`), a malformed list, an unknown role, scope or source, a scope that is not exactly
  `platform`, `products:*` or lower-case `product:<slug>`, a role that does not fit its scope (only
  `product_admin` takes a product scope) and areas on any role but `product_admin`; NULL
  `areas_json` means every area, `[]` means none and is dropped. `stmtInsertBinding` refuses to
  write any of these, and an email row without an expiry, as a second line of defence.
  `listPendingInvites` treats a NULL `expires_at` as expired.
- **A missing table narrows, never locks out.** If `console_role_bindings` does not exist (code
  deployed before its migration), `listAccountGrants` answers no stored grants, so root operators
  keep working; a binding-only member is simply a stranger until the migration lands.
- **Finding 1 (review): a Platform admin binding could mint a root token.** `tokenSession` gives
  every `pkeya_` token the root group, and `POST /tokens` was a `platform` row with step-up, which
  Platform admin holds, so a stepped-up `platform_admin` binding could mint a token that then acted
  as Superadmin on any product. Fix: `handleApiTokenMint` answers 403 `forbidden` with reason
  `superadmin_only` unless `isSuperadmin(principal)`. Listing and revoking tokens stay `platform`
  rows (a token row carries no owner, labels and times only, and revoking only narrows). Pinned by
  `test/surfaces/console/rbacStoredPrincipal.test.ts` (refused with a binding, 201 for root, the bundle write
  through the minted token unreachable). While `tokenSession` carries the root group, this check is
  the only thing between a Platform admin and root.
- **`products:*` never covers the system product** (`can()` rule 4 is unchanged: a system product is
  evaluated as the platform). A Product admin sees only its products and areas in the dispatcher,
  `/products`, `/attention`, `/search` and `/me.permissions`; `/me.platformAdmin` stays
  `can(platform, "platform")`, true only for Superadmin and Platform admin.
- **Email rows never grant.** An invite row names an address, not an account, so a row whose
  `email_norm` equals the account's email grants nothing; claiming it is ST-31.8's conversion.
- **Tests:** `test/surfaces/console/rbacStoredPrincipal.test.ts` (narrowed areas with the refusal naming the area,
  `products:*` and the system product, Platform admin, Console access, a stranger, root plus a
  binding, deletion on the next request and at 30 s, a disabled account, email rows, another
  account's binding, a malformed row, a v1 cookie and a token, a forged signed v1 body naming `aid` / `sid` / `root`, the
  token-mint refusal, a missing bindings table).

**Residual.** A binding for an account that is later disabled stays in the table; it is inert
because the disabled account cannot hold a session (401 within 30 s), but it grants again if the
account is re-enabled. An account's `sub` (member id) is not its key here: bindings are keyed by the
account id, which the subject receives (the principal does not) and which is never logged or
returned (`accountIdBoundary`). The binding read adds one D1 read to each console request, and
runs before the rate limiter (ST-31.6). Nothing writes bindings yet (ST-31.6 on).

### Console Members: the read API (ST-31.4)

**What arrived.** `GET /manage/api/members` and `GET /manage/api/members/:memberId` (platform scope, area
`members`: Superadmin and Platform admin; a Product admin holds `members` at product scope only and is refused
here). Session only (no `tokenScope`). Read-only.

**Control.**

- **No account id in a body.** A person is a `memberId` (`mbr_`, one-way), a display name and an address. The
  handler joins on account ids internally and serialises none (`consoleMembers.test.ts` scans both routes,
  the list also joins `accountIdBoundary.test.ts`; the OpenAPI schemas declare no account id property).
- **The path id is never decoded.** The handler computes the id of each candidate member and compares; a
  malformed, forged, stale or non-member id is the same 404.
- **The directory answers only for the ids it is handed.** `consoleDirectory(accountIds)` reads accounts and
  console links for exactly the accounts that hold a binding or the root rule, so a non-member is never read,
  counted or named. A person with a role is listed; a signed-in person with none is not.
- **Root holders use the principal's own rule.** `consoleRootHolders` applies `rootRuleHolds` with
  `ADMIN_SESSION_TTL_SECONDS` (the constant the principal uses), on active accounts, and only on the account's
  most recently used strong link (as `consoleSubject` does). Each holder also passes `erasureVerdict` (cached
  30 s), and `consoleDirectory` skips accounts on the erasure ledger, so the roster cannot show a Superadmin
  the principal would not treat as one (ST-31.4 fix round; tested in `consoleMembers.test.ts`).
- **An unreadable ledger is said, not hidden.** When `erasureVerdict` answers `unavailable` for an account (R2
  failure or no bucket), the roster leaves that account out and sets `incomplete: true`, so a list that looks
  whole never silently drops a Superadmin; `GET /members/:memberId` answers 503, not 404, for an id it did not
  find while `incomplete` (`consoleMembers.test.ts`).
- **Granter names.** `grantedBy` / `invitedBy` name a granter only while they are a member; a former member is
  `{ name: null }`, so the roster does not become a lookup of departed people.
- **Last sign-in** is the newest `admin.signin` under the member id or any console IdP subject of the account
  (the `consoleActorAliases` set), through `idx_platform_audit_action`; chunked under D1's bound-parameter
  limit.
- **Bounds.** At most 500 members' worth of root holders, 2000 binding rows and 500 invites are read.
- **Disclosure, deliberately.** A Platform admin or Superadmin sees every member's name, address, roles and
  last sign-in, and every open invite's address (`docs/PRIVACY.md`, "What an admin can see"). Product-scoped
  members appear here too; the page is the platform's roster.

### Console Members: the product read and `/access/admins` from bindings (ST-31.5)

**What arrived.** `GET /manage/api/products/:slug/members` (product scope, area `members`; session only) and
`GET /access/admins` now answers from stored bindings and the root rule, no longer from the audit trail.

**Control.**

- **Area gate.** The dispatcher loads the product (404) and checks `members` on it (403), so a narrowed admin
  without `members` is refused (`consoleProductMembers.test.ts`).
- **No account id.** Both bodies name a person by member id, display name and address only; the account id is
  a join key inside the handler (`accountIdBoundary.test.ts` reads the product route).
- **Platform admins are never named**, by either route: they hold no product area, and naming them would
  disclose nothing the asker can use. `products:*` admins appear only in the product route's read-only
  `platformRoles`, not in `/access/admins`.
- **No slug oracle in `/access/admins`.** The product is never looked up. A product's admins are read only when
  the caller already holds an area of `product:<slug>` (`can()`); every other caller, for a real or a
  nonexistent slug, gets the Superadmins alone. Equal answers are tested. (The dispatcher's own 404-before-403
  on `/products/:slug/*` is the older behaviour and unchanged.)
- **Real Superadmins.** The source is `consoleRootHolders` (the principal's own rule) plus stored platform
  Superadmin bindings, both on active accounts. The old rule counted every recent `admin.signin` actor, which
  could name a person the principal no longer treats as a Superadmin.
- **An unreadable ledger is said, not hidden.** Both bodies carry `incomplete: true` when the erasure ledger
  could not be read for an account (an uncached root-only holder included: `consoleRootHolders` keeps every
  account the ledger has not said is erased, and the directory read drops and flags the unreadable ones).
- **Bounded.** At most three people are named; the product route reads at most 500 bindings, 500 invites and
  the 200 stored Superadmin rows.

**`/account-tokens` (ST-31.2 re-review item; closed in the ST-31.4 fix round).** It stays a `platform` row, but the
holder's address is returned to a Superadmin only, in the list and in the DELETE response (`email: null` for a
Platform admin). Most holders are product customers, not console members, and the Platform admin has no consent
to see them. Revoking works by token id; the label, last four characters and times identify the token. Tested in
`consoleMembers.test.ts`. No account id, token or hash is returned.

**Residual.** The rosters are capped (500 members, 500 invites, 2000 bindings) and answer `truncated: true` when a cap
cuts them; `GET /members/<id>` reads up to 20000 bindings so a real member past the cap is still found. A binding for
a disabled account is listed with `disabled: true` (inert; the account cannot sign in).

### Console grant rules (ST-31.3)

**What arrived.** `core/rbac/grantRules.ts`: pure functions that answer who may hand out, take back
or edit a console role binding (ST-28 §2.3, §2.5). They are written out apart from `can()`, which
answers "may this member act" and not "may this member give that away".

**Control.**

- **G1 to G4 as built.** G1: a Product admin grant needs `members` edit at the scope and Product
  admin there with areas covering every area asked for; NULL (every area) needs a granter whose
  own coverage there is every area. G2: Superadmin, Platform admin and anything at `products:*`
  only a Superadmin grants (a Platform admin granting Superadmin to itself is this rule). G3:
  Console access by anyone with `members` edit at platform scope or on a product other than the
  system product. G4: `isWidening` marks a new binding, a different role or scope, a wider list
  and a list turned into NULL as widening (the step-up trigger); `confirmLevel` is L2 for
  Superadmin, Platform admin and `products:*`.
- **Every function fails closed.** A `null` granter, a target that `validateGrant` refuses (shape,
  role, scope, role/scope mismatch, missing `areas`, `product:<system>`, upper case, a slug over
  the P0-14 rule), or a scope the function does not know is refused. The one exception is a
  Superadmin revoking a stored row that no longer validates. An unreadable `after` counts as
  widening and an unreadable `before` as nothing held.
- **Coverage is a union.** The areas of every product admin grant that reaches a scope (its own
  `product:<slug>` and `products:*`) add up; NULL comes only from a grant whose `areas` is NULL,
  never from the sum of lists. The system product's scope is skipped for the `members` check.
- **D-c rulings.** Revoking or narrowing needs `members` edit at the scope with areas covering the
  binding's, with three departures. (1) A `products:*` binding is revoked or narrowed by a
  Superadmin alone (review B1: a `products:*` holder could otherwise strip a peer holder). (2)
  Console access is revoked only with platform `members`, so a Product admin cannot remove a person
  from the console. (3) Only a Superadmin removes a row that does not validate. Revoking
  `product:<slug>` bindings follows the cover rule.
- **G2's "edit console.access"** is the SSO-rules setting, not the Console access role.
- **Edits.** `mayChange(granter, before, after)` is `mayRevoke(before)` and, when `isWidening`,
  `mayGrant(after)`. Checking the grant alone lets `alpha [members, ship]` rewrite
  `alpha [core, keys]` to `alpha [ship]`, dropping areas it does not hold; `mayChange` refuses it.
- **Tests:** `test/core/rbacGrantRules.test.ts` (a hand-written oracle, 8 granters by every target, a
  soundness cross-check against `can()`, the named cases above); reviewer probes over 1.4M granter
  and target combinations found no widening beyond `can()`.

**Residual.**

- The grant handlers (ST-31.6, below) call the engine.
- A handler must combine the checks: `mayChange` for an edit, `mayRevoke` for a delete,
  `mayGrant` for a create, plus the step-up from `isWidening` and `confirmLevel`. Calling one
  alone is the gap.
- The checks never see the grantee or the expiry. They cannot tell who receives a grant or how
  long it lasts; the handler owns that.
- **D-g: no self-grants.** A grant whose grantee is the granter is refused. The engine cannot see
  the grantee, so the handlers enforce it (ST-31.6, below).

### Console role bindings: writes (ST-31.6)

**What arrived.** The first writes of `console_role_bindings`: `POST /manage/api/bindings`,
`PATCH|DELETE /manage/api/bindings/:id` (platform scope, area `members`) and their product twins
`POST /manage/api/products/:slug/members` and `PATCH|DELETE .../members/:bindingId` (product scope,
area `members`, D-d). Session only: no row names a `tokenScope`, so a `pkeya_` token is refused
before a handler runs. `handlers/bindings.ts` holds every check; the twins are thin callers.

**Control, in the order the handler applies it.**

1. **Identity of the writer.** A signed-in account with a member id (`aid` and an `mbr_` sub). A
   v1 cookie has neither and cannot be told apart from its grantee, so it writes nothing. The
   member id is the audit actor and `granted_by`.
2. **Write budget.** `adminGrantWrite`, 30 writes per 5 minutes per member, **failing closed**: a
   limiter outage refuses, it does not leave grants unmetered.
3. **Shape.** Only the fields named; an unknown field (a `member` or `role` on a PATCH, a `scope`
   on a twin) is a 422, so a change of grantee, role or scope is never an edit: it is a new grant.
   `validateGrant` fixes role, scope and areas.
4. **The engine, never `can()`.** `mayGrant` for a POST (G1, G2, G3), `mayChange` for a PATCH,
   `mayRevoke` for a DELETE (D-c; a `products:*` binding and any Superadmin or Platform admin
   binding are a Superadmin's alone). The route table cannot tell a Platform admin from a
   Superadmin, so a Platform admin that reaches `/bindings` is refused every target but Console
   access (`reason: grant_refused`, a 403 that is not `no_access`). An unreadable stored row is
   cleared by a Superadmin only.
5. **The target exists.** A product scope names a real product that is not the system product
   (no bindings for future slugs, so a later product with that slug inherits nothing). The
   engine runs first, so a caller who may not grant learns nothing about which slugs exist.
6. **L2.** `confirmLevel` L2 targets (Superadmin, Platform admin, `products:*`) need
   `confirm: "L2"` in the body (422 `confirm_required`). A UI confirm alone is not a control.
7. **The grantee.** Found by computing each candidate's member id over accounts that hold a
   binding or the root rule (the id is one-way, as `GET /members/:id`), so the endpoint cannot be
   used to look up anyone else. The erasure ledger is read first (`erasureVerdict`: erased is a
   404, unavailable is a 503), then a disabled account is refused (409). **D-g:** the writer is
   never the grantee of a grant or of a widening, a Superadmin included (`reason: self_grant`).
   Taking your own access back is allowed, with one limit: `mayRevoke` still decides, so a Platform
   admin cannot remove its own `platform_admin` binding (D-c: that binding is a Superadmin's to
   remove). Narrowing your own Product admin binding is allowed.
8. **Step-up (G4).** POST rows carry `stepUp` in the route table (so it runs before the handler).
   A PATCH checks it in the handler, after authorization, and only when `isWidening`; narrowing
   and DELETE need none. `STEP_UP_ROUTES` lists the two `(body)` rows and `rbacRouteMatrix`
   keeps the list and the table in step.
9. **CSRF** is the dispatcher's, before the match, for every session mutation.

**Commit and audit.** The change and its audit rows are one batch: `rbac.grant` or `rbac.revoke`
(a widening edit is a grant, a narrowing one a revoke) to `platform_audit`, and to the product's
`audit` for a product scope or a product route, through `core/audit.ts`. PATCH and DELETE carry a
guard on the `areas_json` the caller authorised against, on both the change and its audit rows: a
concurrent edit makes the second a 409 (`changed`) that writes neither. A duplicate
`(account, role, scope)` is a 409 with the existing binding's id (also when the unique index
catches a race). Rows name the grantee by member id only.

**G5 notice.** After the commit, the grantee and every Superadmin (root holders and stored
bindings, active accounts) are emailed through `core/notify` as Polaris Key
(`sender.audience: "operator"`): the change, the role, the scope, the areas and who did it; no link
and no token. At most 25 addresses. Best effort: a failed or suppressed address never undoes the
change, and the response counts (`notified: {sent, of, nobodyNotified}`), never lists, recipients.
With email off the change stands and the response says nobody was notified. The writer is mailed
when it is a Superadmin, which is the point against a stolen session.

**Revocation.** A deleted binding stops granting on the next request (the principal reads bindings
on every request, ST-31.2); a disabled account and a cookie's 30 s live check are unchanged.

**Tests:** `test/surfaces/console/consoleBindingWrites.test.ts`; `rbacRouteMatrix` (the two new step-up rows and the
six rows against the eight principals), `rbacRouteAreas`, `routeCoverage`, `accountIdBoundary`.

**Residual.**

- **Notice, not approval.** A stolen Superadmin session that completes a step-up can still grant
  and revoke; G5 makes it loud, not impossible. The step-up needs a sign-in the IdP proved.
- **A grantee must already hold a role or the root rule.** A person with no binding is reached by
  an invite (ST-31.7), not here.
- **Invites** are not edited or revoked by the 31.6 handlers (email rows answered 404 there);
  31.7 adds cancellation (below). An invite is still not editable: cancel and invite again.
- **Grant/revoke asymmetry.** A Product admin can grant Console access through the product twin
  (G3) but cannot take it back (D-c: platform-scope Console access is removed with platform
  `members`). The Members UI (31.14) must not offer that revoke to a Product admin.
- **The L2 `confirm` field** is a server-side acknowledgement, not an interactive challenge. The
  UI slices decide what the person types.
- **Mail volume.** One change mails up to 25 addresses and the write budget allows 30 changes per
  5 minutes per member, which alone would be about 9,000 mails an hour. ST-31.7 closes it with a
  per-recipient budget on every operator notice (`emailOperatorNoticeHour`, 10 notices per address
  per hour, sharded, failing closed): a notice over budget counts as not sent in `notified`, and
  the change stands. The G5 notice of an L2 change (a grant, widening or revocation of Superadmin,
  Platform admin or `products:*`) is sent with `priority` and skips that budget, so cheap invitations
  cannot silence it; those writes are Superadmin-only, step-up and bounded by the write budget. The
  residual is L1: a Superadmin's inbox receives at most 10 L1 notices an hour (member grants,
  invitations and their digests) plus the L2 notices, whoever causes them.

### Console invitations (ST-31.7)

**What arrived.** `POST /manage/api/bindings` and `POST /manage/api/products/:slug/members` also take
`emails` (exactly one of `member` and `emails`), and `DELETE` takes an invitation back. An invitation is
a `console_role_bindings` row with `email_norm` and no account, which expires 7 days after it is
made (inviting again renews it). **It grants nothing**: the principal reads account rows only, and
turning an invitation into a binding at sign-in is ST-31.8 (verified email, strong sign-in).

**Control.** The 31.6 order applies once to the one grant the addresses share (writer, write budget,
shape, `mayGrant`, target, L2 `confirm`), so an invitation is held to exactly what a member grant is
(G1, G2, G3; an SM-7-class role, i.e. a platform role or `products:*`, is stored and flagged
`needsOperatorSignIn`). Then per address:

1. **Shape.** At most 20 addresses; each one `strictEmail` (trimmed, lower-cased); a repeat is
   `merged`, a non-address `invalid`; a non-string is a 422 for the whole request.
2. **D-g.** The writer's session address, or any address on the writer's account (every link email
   and the primary email, verified or not, read through Identity's `public.ts`), refuses the whole
   request (`self_grant`): an invitation to yourself is a grant to yourself. A D-e match on the
   writer's own account is refused the same way. D-g at creation is partial (an address linked
   later is not seen); conversion re-checks it (31.8).
3. **D-e.** An address that is the verified primary email of exactly one active, ledger-clear account that already holds a
   binding or the root rule gets an account binding (`updated`, or `exists`). Anything else is
   `invited`, including an address that matches two members (not guessed at), an unverified
   address, a disabled account and an erased one. An erasure-ledger outage is a 503 and writes
   nothing.
4. **Invitation budget.** `adminInviteAddress`: 100 addresses per member per hour, counted per
   distinct valid address whether or not it is a member (so the 429 does not reveal membership),
   failing closed; a request that would exceed it is refused whole (429 `invite_budget`) and
   writes nothing.
5. **Re-invite.** Inviting an address that already has an invite renews it only for a writer who
   could cancel it (D-c, `mayRevoke`); otherwise the answer is `exists` and nothing is written or
   mailed. A renewal audits the `before`.

**Commit and audit.** One batch: the rows and one `rbac.invite` (invite) or `rbac.grant` (update)
audit row each, to `platform_audit` and, for a product scope or route, the product's `audit`. An
invitee is named in the audit trail by an opaque reference (`invitee:` and the first 12 hex digits of
the peppered recipient hash), never by address; the address lives only in the invite row, which the
nightly job deletes 7 days after it expired (`purgeExpiredInvites`, a step of `scheduled.ts`), and an
account erasure deletes the invites for that account's addresses (`deletion.ts`).
Cancelling is `DELETE` (D-c / B1 apply; the product twin reaches only its own product's rows) and
writes `rbac.revoke`.

**What the email is.** A Polaris Key operator notice (`sender.audience: "operator"`) to the invited
address only, naming the inviter, role, scope and areas. The link is the console sign-in page with
`login_hint=<address>`: no token, code or id. It cannot sign anyone in or accept anything; a
forwarded mail grants nothing, because conversion (31.8) needs the sign-in to prove that address.
The same link is returned in the response when the mail did not go out (email off, suppressed,
over budget), so it is not a secret either. The Superadmins get one count-only digest per request
(no address). Every operator mail is within the per-recipient hourly budget.

**Abuse controls.** (a) 20 addresses a request; (b) 100 addresses per member per hour;
(c) the 30-writes-per-5-minutes write budget; (d) 10 operator notices per recipient per hour, so an
invitee cannot be mail-bombed by repeated invitations and an inbox cannot be flooded by many
inviters; (e) the platform sender's own suppression list and Apple relay rules; (f) a Superadmin
digest per request, so a hijacked session is loud; (g) L2 confirm, step-up and D-g as for grants.

**Enumeration.** The per-address status (`updated`/`exists` versus `invited`) tells the caller
whether an address belongs to an existing console member. The caller is a signed-in operator who
passed `mayGrant` for this very grant, the step-up and the budgets, and a Platform admin or
Superadmin can read the full roster anyway. A Product admin could learn that a given address is a
console member elsewhere; it can already invite it, and the answer reveals no role, scope or id
(no member id or account id is in the response). The budget of 100 addresses an hour bounds a probe
to that rate. Accepted residual; a stricter variant would answer `invited` for both and write the
binding anyway.

**Residual.**

- **Invite hijack.** Whoever controls the invited mailbox and can sign in with that verified
  address converts the invitation (31.8). That is the intended model; an SM-7 role additionally
  needs the operator sign-in. Cancel an invitation sent to a wrong address.
- **Mail from the Polaris Key sender is attacker-steerable text** (the inviter's display name is
  sanitised by `displayValue`; the role, scope and areas are enumerated values). Capped as above.
- A forwarded invitation mail reveals that a Polaris Key console invitation exists for that
  address, nothing more.
- The invitation budget is per member, not platform-wide.
- **Sub-addressing** (`a+1@`, `a+2@`) gets past the per-recipient cap for one mailbox; it is bounded
  by the per-member invitation budget.
- **Writer-controlled text in mail** (the inviter's name, a product name) is neutralised by
  `operatorText`: URL schemes are dropped and domain-like tokens are defanged (`example[.]com`) so
  mail clients do not auto-link them. Residual: plain prose can still mislead.
- **Erasure** deletes invites only for the erased account's verified addresses; an address the
  account merely claimed leaves the invitee's invite alone.

**Tests:** `test/surfaces/consoleInvites.test.ts`; `test/surfaces/console/consoleBindingWrites.test.ts` (the per-recipient
budget on G5 notices, fail-closed guarded writes); `routeCoverage`, `accountIdBoundary`, `scheduled`.

### Sign-in gate and invite conversion (ST-31.8)

**What arrived.** Console membership is "holds a grant". The callback's **pre-gate** runs before
anything is written and admits three people: the root rule (the platform admin group), a known
console link whose account holds a stored account binding, and an identity the IdP vouched an
address for at this sign-in (`email` and `email_verified`, from a provider that may vouch) that has
an unexpired invite. The last is admitted to the sign-in only. After `consoleSignIn` (the SM rules
unchanged) `convertInvites` runs, then the **post-gate** re-resolves the principal: no grant ends the
new session row and refuses with the same card, before any cookie exists. A repeat sign-in has no
invite left and converts nothing. Also in this slice: a `/products/:slug/*` route answers an unknown
