`default`), for opening only. The operator procedure is RUNBOOK "Rotating when the old KEK is
unknown". Controls:

- **It never seals.** `PLATFORM_KEK_ACTIVE` must name a `PLATFORM_KEK_KEYS` entry, checked before
  the legacy key joins, and the legacy key is imported without the `encrypt` usage, so no path
  can seal under it.
- **No silent choice.** The same kid in both shapes with different bytes refuses to load the ring
  (fail closed: `503` on the keyring endpoint, every product route 404s) instead of picking one.
  A precedence rule would orphan one set of blobs, chosen by a rule an operator mid-rotation is
  unlikely to know. Equal keys, compared as decoded bytes, are accepted.
- **No key material in diagnostics.** The configuration error (also raised on Platform →
  Settings as `kek_keyring_unusable`), the `kek_legacy_open_only` warning, the endpoint's
  `legacy` block and the console name kids and counts only. The sealed `SIGNIN_*` Worker
  secrets are reported by name when their envelope names the legacy kid; the kid is read from
  the envelope and nothing is opened.
- **A bounded life.** The `kek_legacy_open_only` warning stays while `PLATFORM_KEK` is the only
  source of its kid (not for a same-bytes copy of a `PLATFORM_KEK_KEYS` entry), and the endpoint
  reports `legacy.remaining` (stored values under the legacy kid), `legacy.workerSecrets` and
  `safeToDelete`, the gate for deleting it.

**Residual risk.** (1) Re-sealing does not erase old ciphertext: D1 backups and Time Travel from
before the sweep still hold blobs under the old key, so whoever holds that key and such a dump
reads them. If the old key may have leaked, this is the KEK compromise case (RUNBOOK,
containment): the rotation runs the same steps, and every product signing key sealed under the
old key is rotated as well. (2) Deleting `PLATFORM_KEK` while a value is still under it makes
that value dark (its product 404s, or a sign-in provider leaves the login card). `safeToDelete`
is the gate, and the operator applies it; the Worker cannot stop a `wrangler secret delete`.
(3) The legacy key adds no new writer: whoever can set Worker secrets could already replace the
whole ring. (4) A `PLATFORM_KEK` left beside a ring re-admits the key it holds for opening,
under the legacy kid, even after that kid is retired from `PLATFORM_KEK_KEYS`. The kid stays
open-capable until `PLATFORM_KEK` is deleted, and while it does, an early retirement reads
`unopenable: 0`, so the re-check cannot catch it. The RUNBOOK's retirement step therefore
deletes `PLATFORM_KEK` in the same `wrangler secret bulk` call that drops the kid ("Rotating
PLATFORM_KEK", step 8), or, if that was missed, deletes it only once `legacy.safeToDelete` is
true. In the KEK compromise case this matters more: while
`PLATFORM_KEK` holds the leaked key, that key still opens, so whoever holds it and can write to
D1 can plant a value the Worker accepts. The containment steps (RUNBOOK, "KEK compromise
(containment)") delete `PLATFORM_KEK`, and containment is not complete until `legacy` is gone
from the keyring endpoint.

### Offline grace clamped to licence expiry (LX-07)

S-19 G9: `graceUntil = issuedAt + maxOfflineDays × 86 400` was never bounded by the licence, so a
licence expiring tomorrow with 30 offline days kept an install that stayed offline running for 30
days, and an offline bundle minted with `graceDays: 365` for a licence expiring next week ran for
a year. For an offline install the grace bound is the only revocation lever (WIRE-CONTRACT-V4
§4.3), so this was the whole of a time-limited licence's enforcement offline.

- **The clamp.** While the product's `licensing.clampGraceToExpiry` is on (the registry default),
  every document a licence grants is stamped `graceUntil = min(window, max(expires_at,
expiresAt))` (`core/licensing/graceClamp.ts`, `core/documents.ts` `clampGraceUntil`): the licence
  document, the config document of a device R1 binds to its licence (its secrets stop with the
  licence offline as well as online), both inner documents of an offline bundle, and Identity's
  fused browser-session document. One function computes it for all four, so no path can drift.
- **The floor is `expiresAt`, not `expires_at`.** Every verifier refuses `graceUntil < expiresAt`,
  so a licence that expires within the hour gets a document valid for its ordinary hour. Residual:
  an install can run up to one hour past the licence's expiry, the same hour any freshly fetched
  document has; the licence route refuses the next fetch (`licenseUsable`).
- **Fail-safe direction.** The setting is resolved through ST-04's resolver (an expired
  break-glass claim is no claim); anything but an explicit `false`, including an unknown product
  or an unreadable row, reads on, which only ever shortens a window. The opt-out is a critical
  setting: a console change needs a reason and is audited (`setting.update`), and a manifest value
  is visible in the repository.
- **What it does not cover.** A device that holds a document issued before the clamp keeps that
  document's window until it reconnects; an online device re-fetches within the hour (the
  half-life rule, WIRE-CONTRACT-V4 §5). A clock rolled back on the device defeats any
  `graceUntil`, clamped or not (§6 below). A grant's own expiry is not applied to the window
  (S-19 §7.6: that would end base access offline); per-entry expiry for add-on grants is
  LX-18/LX-19's wire work.
- **No wire change.** No claim is added or renamed; `graceUntil` only takes an earlier value
  inside the range verifiers already enforce (`[expiresAt, issuedAt + MAX_GRACE_SECONDS]`), as
  §3.6's informative note says.
- **The affected-licence report** (`graceClampReport`, `scripts/grace-clamp-report.ts`) runs on
  an offline copy, writes nothing (checked) and carries licence ids, tiers and counts only: no
  name, email or key.

### Licence and add-on lifecycle (LX-12)

A licence's `status` stays `active`/`disabled`; `ended_reason` records why it ended (`revoked`,
`superseded`, `refunded`, `chargeback`). A grant (an add-on) is `active`, `past_due`,
`suppressed`, `revoked` or `refunded`. Both state machines are one table each
(`core/licensing/lifecycle.ts`), and every writer's SQL is derived from them
(`lifecycleWrites.ts`).

- **The database cannot take a transition the table lacks.** Each UPDATE is guarded by its
  event's source states, so a stale read or a concurrent write changes nothing rather than
  moving a row along a missing edge. An operator's Enable that races a refund finds the row
  refunded and leaves it. A test runs every cell of both tables against SQLite.
- **No refund grace.** A full refund or a chargeback ends the item in the second it is written.
  The contribution predicate reads only `state` and `expires_at`, never `grace_until`, so no
  value in that column can extend access. `licensing.refundGraceHours` is still registered and
  has no effect (LX-40 removes it). A partial refund never reaches the lifecycle.
- **An operator cannot undo a refund.** Enable on a refunded or charged-back licence answers 409
  and writes nothing, and `reinstate` of a refunded grant is refused. Only the store's reversal
  of that refund or chargeback restores the item. To give access anyway an operator issues a new
  licence or add-on, which is its own audited act.
- **A store's reversal cannot lift an operator's end.** A refund or chargeback reversal moves only
  an item that money ended. An item an operator revoked, a merge superseded or a support action
  suppressed stays ended.
- **Money ends are recorded over other ends.** A refund or chargeback of an item an operator has
  already ended replaces that reason, so the record always shows that the money went back.
  Residual: one reason column holds one end, so a reversal can reinstate an item that a second
  end should keep ended. Three orders do it:
  - an operator ends the item, then it is refunded: the refund replaces the operator's reason;
  - it is refunded, then an operator revokes it: the revoke changes nothing (`same`);
  - it is refunded, then charged back, or the other way round: the second money end changes
    nothing. A grant records both as `refunded`.

  In each case a later reversal of the recorded money end reinstates the item, although the
  operator's end or the other money end still stands. The audit log keeps every step. Today
  nothing writes a reversal through the lifecycle, so this cannot happen yet. Once CM-22 wires
  store reversals it becomes a real fail-open. **CM-22 acceptance: a reversal must never lift an
  operator end or a standing chargeback** (for example by keeping every end an item has, not one
  reason).

- **Store grants keep their own writer.** Until LX-11 retires the dual-write, a store grant's
  state is the projection of `license_store_grants`, so the lifecycle's grant writers exclude
  store sources: an operator cannot reinstate a refunded store purchase through them. Store
  refunds still revoke through `applyStoreGrant`, as `revoked`, until CM-22 routes them through
  the lifecycle as `refunded`. The `oidc` grant's sign-in upsert also writes `active` on every
  sign-in. Nothing suppresses or refunds an `oidc` grant yet; the package that adds an operator's
  suppress (LX-13, LX-14) must make that upsert keep `suppressed`.
- **No wire change.** A disabled licence's document request gets the same 401 whatever its
  reason (tested). The reason reaches devices only with LX-18's wire amendment. `ended_reason` and
  `superseded_by` are licence metadata, not personal data, and stay on a deleted product's
  licences with the rest of their shape.

### Identity consolidation (I-27)

plans/I-27.md §6: one row per threat, each written by the package that builds it.

- **Rogue connection (I-30; I-32 for product scope).** A connection is an upstream OIDC provider
  the platform signs people in through (`identity_connections`). Only a platform admin creates or
  changes a platform connection (I-31's console; until then only the `source: env` seed of the
  `PLATFORM_OIDC_*` trio exists). A product connection is tenant-scoped: it signs in only inside
  its product (`tenant_scope = product:<slug>`), its issuer must pass `OIDC_ISSUER_ALLOWLIST`, its
  audience is always `customers` (a table CHECK), and it never vouches for an address, so its
  identities always meet the email gate's code (`connectionVouchesForEmail`, tests). An operator
  audience (`operators`, `both`) is a platform connection's only, and a console write of either
  is refused until ST-32's Superadmin gate; the env seed is exempt.
- **Domain takeover or lapse (I-30).** A domain counts only once a TXT record at
  `_pkey-challenge.<domain>` holds `pkey-domain-verification=<token>`, with one random token per
  connection and domain, so one connection's record proves nothing for another
  (`services/identity/connections/domains.ts`). Domains are exact: `example.com` never covers
  `sub.example.com`, `evil-example.com` or `example.com.evil.net`, and a domain or address that is
  not plain ASCII before it is lower-cased is refused, so a lookalike (the Kelvin sign folds into
  `k` under `toLowerCase`, a Cyrillic letter, a punycode label) never matches a verified domain.
  Each `(scope, domain)` has at most one verified owner: a second connection's proof is refused as
  taken, and a partial unique index backs the rule. The maintenance cron re-checks every verified
  domain daily: an answer without the token unverifies it at once, and resolver errors keep the
  state for 72 hours after the last conclusive answer, then unverify it. An unverified domain does
  not route, vouch or enforce (tests: verified, absent and erroring answers, the 72-hour lapse,
  takeover with the other connection's record and with its own, subdomain, suffix and homograph).
  Residual: whoever controls a domain's DNS controls its proof, which is the point; a registrar
  or DNS-provider compromise is out of scope, and the window after a hostile DNS change is at most
  one day.
- **Group and claim injection (I-30; LX-36 and ST-32 read them).** Groups and access-rule claims
  come only from the claims a connection's claim map names, in an ID token the one client verified
  (signature, `iss`, exact `aud` and `azp`, nonce, freshness). Groups are capped at 100 names, each
  a printable name; claims are kept only for the names the map lists under `claims[]`. Both are
  replaced at every sign-in through the link, in one `UPDATE` (`groups_json`, `claims_json`), and
  every group or claim rule names its connection, so one IdP's `groups` never satisfies a rule
  written for another. A connection's `name`, `picture` and `birthdate` feed only the sign-in's
  imported profile and are never stored on the link.
- **The rewritten `/callback` (I-30).** Every connection, the env-seeded platform IdP included,
  finishes at `/callback`, whose flow record (single-use, bound to the starting browser) names the
  connection. The seeded row first applies I-17's policy (`ended` refuses, `operators-only`
  refuses an unknown subject); every identity then goes through `beginProviderSignIn`, so an
  address the connection does not vouch for meets the email gate's code and never lands on an
  email-less account. Because the seeded row has no verified domain, Pocket ID vouches for no
  address on the card and `/callback` until a domain is verified: a known link whose account has
  a confirmed email signs in as before, and anyone else sees one email code (announced in the
  release notes). The legacy product callback keeps today's rule until I-32b (the I-17 section).
  The seeded row is the only source for the card and `/callback` from this release: a changed
  `PLATFORM_OIDC_*` does not rewrite it, and its client secret is sealed under `PLATFORM_KEK` with
  the AAD `pkey:v2:_platform:identity-connection:<id>`. The session's `amr` is
  `connection:<id>`.
- **SSRF (I-30).** Discovery, the JWKS, the token request and the DNS-over-HTTPS lookups all go
  through the one gated fetch (`core/oidc/client.ts`): `https:` only, no credentials in the URL,
  the default port only, no private, loopback, link-local or reserved address literal, and a host
  on the relying party's own allowlist (a connection's issuer host and its configured `jwks_uri`
  host; `cloudflare-dns.com` alone for domain proofs). A URL inside a discovery document on any
  other host is refused, not followed; redirects are never followed; bodies are capped and every
  call has a timeout. Keys are verified with jose's `createLocalJWKSet` over the gated JWKS;
  `createRemoteJWKSet`, which dialled outside any guard, is gone (a source test). Product issuers
  are tenant-supplied and must also pass `OIDC_ISSUER_ALLOWLIST`.
- **Routing enumeration (I-30).** `POST /api/signin/email/start` routes an address to a connection
  when its domain is verified by an active connection whose audience covers the surface. The
  answer (`next: {kind: "sso", connection: {id, label}, enforced}`) depends on the domain only,
  never on whether an account exists (a test compares the bytes for a known and an unknown address
  in the same domain, routed, enforced and unrouted), and the start keeps its Turnstile check and
  rate limits. A routed start sends no email until the person picks the code; an enforced domain
  never gets an email code or magic link, at the start, on resend, or when an earlier code is
  redeemed after the domain became enforced. What routing reveals is that a domain uses single
  sign-on, which its verification already made public in DNS.

- **Auto-link through a verified domain (I-30; Owner decisions Q1, 2026-10-08).** The rule "never
  join by email match" is narrowed to one case (`connections/autoLink.ts`): a sign-in through a
  PLATFORM connection whose address is inside one of its DNS-verified domains with
  `email_verified`, for an identity with no link yet, where exactly one active account has
  verified that exact address. The identity is then linked to that account, every verified
  address of the account is mailed ("<label> was connected to your Polaris Key account"), and the
  link is audited (`account.link.auto`). A product connection, an unverified domain, a subdomain or
  lookalike, an unverified claim, or an address on two accounts never auto-links: those keep the
  email gate's join offer, with proof of both identities (tests). Residual: the domain's IdP is
  trusted for its own domain's addresses, which is what verifying the domain asserts; an IdP that
  mints `email_verified` for an address it does not control can take over that address's account,
  so only platform admins verify domains, and the mail tells the owner at once.
- **Birth date (I-33).** `accounts.birthdate` and `birthdate_source` (`accounts/birthdate.ts`).
  Never released to an app, and never stored without the person's acceptance.
  - _Stored only on acceptance._ A connection's mapped `birthdate` claim rides only in the
    sign-in's gate record (I-02's store, 15 minutes, deleted when the gate passes), as
    FinishStep's offer. The account gets it only when the person accepts it there (source
    `connection:<id>`, or `user` once edited), or adds it in Account → Profile. A date nobody
    offered is refused (`birthdate_not_offered`), and so is any value that is not a real calendar
    date from 1900-01-01 to tomorrow in UTC (`invalid_birthdate`, strict `YYYY-MM-DD`; a
    withheld-year or year-only claim is never offered). A refused submission writes nothing
    (tests).
  - _Never released._ The person's own `GET /api/me/profile` is the one route that answers it. No
    consent item, device response, signed document, developer API, Users page, developer export
    or `id_token` carries it, whatever the person consented to (a grant naming `birthdate` changes
    nothing). Tests: every recorded transcript and its Godot mirror; the console's Users list,
    search, row, export and events, its licence and device pages and Activity; the device routes
    and the signed licence document. A source test allows the name only in the profile, FinishStep
    and the account lifecycle files, so a new reader is a reviewed change.
  - _Never kept elsewhere._ Not on a sign-in method (`account_links`), not in the audit (the
    profile audit row names the field, never the value), not in mail, not in a log line (tests).
    A join fills it on the survivor only when the survivor has none, with its source, and the
    join's undo takes back exactly what it filled; the undo snapshot holds it for at most 72 hours.
    Deleting the account clears it at once, before the erasure finishes.
  - _Not built._ Age booleans, `minimumAge` and `identity.minimumAge` wait until a product gates
    content: nothing decides anything from a birth date today.
- **Polaris Key's terms (I-33).** `identity.platformTerms` (`core/platformTerms.ts`) is a platform
  setting, unset by default, so no terms step shows and no `_platform` acceptance row is written
  until the owner publishes reviewed terms (I-27 Q2). It widens nothing: it adds a step that every
  new account must pass, and its worst misuse (a wrong version or URL) records a wrong acceptance,
  never access. No console route writes it; a row that is not exactly `{version, termsUrl,
privacyUrl}` with https URLs reads as unset, and an unreadable store fails the sign-in rather
  than creating an account without the acceptance published terms require. The acceptance is
  written in the same batch that creates the account, on both new-account paths (a provider's
  first sign-in and a new address's email code), and records the version the gate opened with.
  Residual: I-30 sends the platform IdP's `/callback` through the gate (an identity with no
  account always opens it), so only the legacy product callback still creates accounts without
  the step until I-32b retires it, and publishing waits for that (docs/RUNBOOK.md).
- **Personal tokens (I-27 §2.5; `admin` scope ST-34.3 to 34.5).** A `pkeyp_` token is a bearer
  credential for one account. `packages:read` is minted in the portal. `admin` is minted nowhere
  but a console-approved `pkey login` (PX-W14's `cli` purpose, above): the poll mints it after a
  stepped-up console session approved the code, never a portal session. **Phishing:** an attacker
  runs `pkey login` on their machine and talks an operator into approving the code, which would
  hand the attacker the operator's console reach for 7 days. Mitigations: the approval is a
  console-only, stepped-up decision (never auto, never a portal session); the card shows the
  machine name, place and the code to compare with the terminal ("Check this matches your
  terminal"); the code lives 5 minutes and is single use; the poll needs the browser binding
  cookie, so a leaked code or handle mints nothing; the token is default-deny on the admin API
  (`personalToken` rows), re-checked against the holder's roles on every use, audited on every use,
  individually revocable by the holder and by Superadmins, and revoked with the account. The
  approver is also sent the new-device security notice. **Residual:** an operator who approves a
  code they did not start, after comparing nothing, is phished; the card copy and the notice are
  the defence.

### App passthrough on authorize and token (I-08)

plans/I-08.md §6, WIRE-CONTRACT-V4 §12.4 and §12.5. An app sends a person's browser to
`GET /<p>/identity/authorize`, the card asks them (Continue, Cancel), and the app redeems the code
at `POST /<p>/identity/token` for a device token. One row per threat; tests are in
`test/surfaces/identityAuthorize.test.ts` and the transcripts `redirect-web-*.json`.

- **Code interception and replay (PKCE, RFC 7636 / 9700).** The code is useless without the
  verifier: `S256` is the only method (`plain` and an absent method are `invalid_request`), the
  challenge is stored hashed as the code's proof, and `token` derives the challenge from the
  presented verifier and redeems in one atomic operation in I-02's store. Match or mismatch, the
  code ends: a wrong verifier burns it (no guessing), a second redemption finds nothing, and the
  code lives 60 seconds. The code is addressed by the product and a peppered hash, bound to the
  `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, account and granted scope, and a mismatch of either is
  `invalid_grant`. Never a token in a URL or fragment: the device token is in the body of the
  `token` response only. Residual: a code stolen from the redirect together with the verifier
  (which never leaves the app) is the app's own compromise.
- **Open redirect and redirect-URI confusion.** A `redirect_uri` must equal the canonical
  `origin + path` built from a registered `web.origins` entry and an `identity.redirectPaths`
  entry, both exact: the URI the app sent must equal the parsed form, so a query, fragment,
  userinfo, port, dot segment, encoded dot, backslash, prefix, suffix or sibling or sub-domain
  never matches (`validateRedirectUri`, tests). `client_id` and `redirect_uri` are checked before
  anything else, and until both are valid the answer is a branded page and never a redirect; every
  later error redirects only to the validated URI. The product's own manifest is the only source of
  both lists.
- **Login CSRF and a forwarded authorize URL (R1-07 for the web redirect).** An attacker who starts
  `authorize` and sends the card URL to a victim gets nothing: the request handle is bound to the
  browser that started it by the `__Host-pk_req` cookie (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax), and
  Continue and Cancel need that binder, the account session and the portal CSRF header; a victim
  without the attacker's binder gets `404 not_found`, the same shape as an unknown handle. The code
  is delivered only by the response to the press and only to the URI the product registered, so the
  attacker never receives it. The other direction (an attacker starts a flow and the victim's
  browser lands on the app with the attacker's code) is the app's `state` check, the contract's
  duty: the attacker's `state` is not the victim session's. A cross-site POST is refused by
  Fetch Metadata. Refused Continues (terms, licence choice, bad consent) consume nothing, and a
  stranger cannot burn a handle.
- **Mix-up (RFC 9207).** `iss` is on every redirect, success and error, and in discovery; the SDK
  compares it with the issuer it started the flow with.
- **No silent grants (D22).** Continue is always shown and records the claims granted (a subset of
  the request's scope; an unknown claim is `invalid_request`) and the hash of what the product
  asked, so a changed ask is asked again. The product's terms are enforced at Continue as well as
  at the email gate: a session that never went through the gate for this product accepts the
  version it was shown or is refused (`terms_required`). The licence choice is never silent: an
  account holding licences for the product must name one (`license_choice_required`).
- **Device takeover at `token`.** `token` takes `X-PKey-Device` and no device credential, so a
  device id is a bearer-less identifier as on `license/activate` and `devices/register`. The
  rules are the same: a device id that already runs on a licence is never taken over without a
  choice; keeping the licence it runs on needs the device's own live token in `Authorization`; a
  seat claim is seat-checked and refuses a device another licence holds. A code holder (a PKCE-
  proven account holder) can therefore bind only their own account to a device id, claim a seat on
  a licence they chose from their own account, or register a licence-less device; they cannot read
  or rotate another device's token. A licence-less device id that already holds a credential is re-registered only with that credential in `Authorization: Bearer` (I-08b); device ids are 128 random bits chosen by the SDK.
- **Brute force and enumeration.** `authorize` 60 a minute per client network; `token` 30 a minute
  per network and 10 a minute per device id, both failing closed, Continue and Cancel 30 a minute
  per account; a malformed code or verifier is refused before the store is touched. Every "no" at
  `token` for a code is one `invalid_grant`. Audit rows (`signin.continue`, `signin.token`) hold the
  subject and device, never a code, verifier, `state`, challenge or hint.
- **Hints.** `login_hint` and `name_hint` prefill the card and verify nothing; they are normalised
  or dropped and never become a session, a verified address or a displayed name the card trusts
  over the account's. The card's app name and icon come from the client record and never from a
  query parameter (PX-W13).
- **The picture and the profile.** The `token` response carries no profile; the claims the person
  consented to are recorded for the ID token of I-21. Nothing here hands an app an account
  session: the first-party session cookie is never accepted on `token` or on any Cloud Sync route.
- **Replace and the choice grant (I-08b).** See the next section.

### Licence choice at sign-in (I-08b)

plans/I-08.md D2, D5, plans/I-04.md §B, §F.3, §G, plans/I-27.md §2.2, WIRE-CONTRACT-V4 §12.4.1 and
§12.5.1. The account's licences for the product are listed on the card, or in the app through a
pending sign-in grant; the person replaces a device, enters a key, or gets the first automatic
licence. Tests are in `test/surfaces/identityChoice.test.ts` and the transcripts `redirect-web-choose*.json`
and `choice-*.json`.

- **The grant (a capability to read and finish a sign-in).** `sg_` and 32 random bytes; only a
  peppered hash is an address in I-02's store (`signin-grant`), so a listing yields nothing
  presentable. 300 seconds, inside the fresh sign-in that Replace treats as its step-up. It exists
  only after `token` redeemed a code with its PKCE verifier, so it is bound to the verifier's
  holder, and it answers only the `X-PKey-Device` that redeemed the code: any other device id is
  `invalid_grant` and does not burn it. It travels in a JSON body, never a URL, and the routes are
  device-facing (no ambient credential for a page to ride on; CORS answers `web.origins` without
  credentials). One grant per code; `complete` takes it atomically, so two concurrent completes
  cannot both bind (of any number, one wins), and `cancel` ends it. A refusal the person can retry
  (a full licence, a lost mint, a wrong key, a budget) puts it back for the time it has left and
  never extends it. 30 view, device and key reads per grant, counted in the store by
  compare-and-set; 60 a minute per client network. Device code never issues a grant: it is the
  cross-device channel that can be phished (R1-07), and a grant there would hand whoever holds the
  code the account's licence and device lists and a Replace the person never sees. Residual: a
  stolen grant is useless without the device id (128 random bits the SDK chose) and expires in five
  minutes; what it shows the app is what the card already showed the person.
- **Enumeration.** The views list only the signed-in account's own licences
  (`licenses.account_id`), never the device's floating licence; the Keep row names no licence.
  `choice/devices` and the card's devices read answer one `404 not_found` for a licence that is
  unknown, another account's, not full, or whose portal is off. Nothing is looked up by a licence
  key except the explicit key choice.
- **Replace (a device leaves, another takes its seat).** The same operation as the portal's Remove
  (`planFreeAccountDevice`): the portal is on, the account owns the licence, the device holds a
  seat on it, the `portalDeviceDisconnect` budget (20 per 60 s per product, account and network) is
  charged after ownership is proven and shared by both surfaces (a blocked Replace is `429` with
  `retryAfter`), the audit row `portal.device.disconnect` reads "to sign in <label>", and the
  `deviceRemovedNotice` security email goes to every verified address. The removal and the new
  device's seat claim commit in one D1 batch, so a lost race leaves both undone; only if the claim
  cannot join the batch does the freed device stay freed (audited, emailed, `racedAfterFree`). The
  card's Continue records the intent, validates it dry (no budget spent), and `token` executes it,
  so a stolen code (60 s, PKCE) cannot Replace without the verifier.
- **The first automatic licence.** Minted by Continue (card) or `choice/complete` `create` (app),
  never by sign-in alone: a usable licence in the account forbids it, except the explicit create
  offered when every candidate is full. Uniqueness is the `license-mint` claim in I-02's store
  (`<product>:` and a peppered hash of the account id, 30 s, written if absent): of two concurrent
  presses one wins, re-reads the offer inside the claim and mints, the other mints nothing and
  answers `409 license_choice_required`; an unreachable store fails closed (`503 unavailable`,
  nothing minted). Discover's claim takes the same claim, so an add racing a Continue mints once.
  LX-38's unique index on `licenses(product, account_id)` replaces the claim and re-runs its test.
  The licence is an account licence (origin `oidc`, `account_id` set in the insert's batch, no
  `sub`, no key), under the same policy (`identityTier`) and provisioning as a sign-in mint.
- **Key entry in the app.** `choice/complete` `key` is PX-W9's key entry on the `app` surface:
  counted exactly once, in the seat claim's own batch, refused with `license_owned` or
  `key_entry_limit` when the licence is in an account or past its limit (while
  `identity.keyEntryRefusals` is on), and the device stays key-bound (a sign-out does not release
  it). The route is a key-guessing oracle, so every attempt spends one of the grant's 30 reads and
  the network's 60 a minute; a wrong key is `401 unauthorized` and keeps the grant. A key is never
  stored on a code (Continue refuses `key`), only presented to the request that binds it.
- **Licence-less takeover at `token`.** A licence-less device id that already holds a credential is
  re-registered only by the device that presents it in `Authorization: Bearer`; without the proof
  `token` answers `403 not_entitled`. Registering rotates the token, so without this a code holder
  could have bound their own account to someone else's licence-less device row.

- **R1-07 for device code.** Device code's own boundary is I-37's explicit approval (see "The
  device-code user-code page" and "Remote phishing"); this section covers the web redirect only.

### Platform → Connections: the operator's side of connections (I-31)

The console adds, changes, turns off and deletes platform connections, claims their email domains
and runs a test sign-in (`console/handlers/platformConnections.ts`,
`services/identity/connections/{admin,testSignIn}.ts`). The attacker is a hostile or careless
operator session, a stolen session, and a hostile issuer an operator is talked into adding.

- **Authority.** Every route is the `platform` area (`ADMIN_ROUTES`, `rbac-route-areas.json`). A
  change (add, change, delete, claim, verify, enforce, release) is a **step-up** write, and a
  token reaches none of them. Discovery and the test are not step-up (they save nothing) but are
  rate-limited per operator (`credentialCheck`, fail closed).
- **Secrets.** A client secret goes in once, is sealed under PLATFORM_KEK with
  `connectionSecretContext(id)`, and is never read back: views carry `hasSecret`, the audit rows
  carry the same boolean, and a test's draft secret is sealed to its flow and lives only in the
  single-use store for ten minutes. `test/surfaces/console/connectionsAdmin.test.ts` greps responses, rows and
  audit text for the plaintext.
- **Issuers (SSRF).** `isSafeIssuerUrl` plus no port; discovery runs through the one gated fetch
  (https, the issuer's host and a `jwks_uri` host only, no redirect, capped, timed out), and a
  document whose endpoints point elsewhere is refused. A row is written only after discovery
  answered. Test: private, loopback, link-local, port, credential, query and non-https issuers
  make no request.
- **Audience.** `operators` and `both` are refused (403 `audience_not_available`) until ST-32's
  Superadmin gate exists. A seeded row keeps its audience; its issuer and client cannot move.
- **Audit.** Each change is one batch with its `platform_audit` row
  (`identity.connection.create|update|rotate_secret|enable|disable|delete|domain_*`), so a change
  cannot land unrecorded (a domain's add, release and enforce included; a verification that finds
  the record gone is audited as `domain_unverify`). No audit field holds a secret. An issuer cannot
  move while people sign in through the connection.
- **Test sign-in (admin-3-19).** The flow is the portal's own with a `test` record: bound to the
  starting browser by the SSO cookie, and its result is read once, by the starting operator's `sub`
  and the wizard's draft id only (a wrong reader leaves it in place). Claims are shown and never
  stored in D1; the preview is the mapped values and claim _names_. A provider's error is plain
  text, capped at 200 characters, control characters removed and secret-shaped runs redacted. The
  same-tab return is one fixed path. A test runs when the portal is off; an ordinary sign-in still
  needs it on.
- **The key-set host and the secret.** A connection may name a `jwks_uri` on a second host, and
  that host joins the gated fetch's allowlist. If the provider's discovery document then names it
  as `token_endpoint`, the code exchange (which carries the client secret) is sent there. The
  operator already trusts the issuer's document; an operator who adds a `jwks_uri` trusts that host
  with the secret too. The console does not offer the field, and the API refuses a non-https or
  private address.
- **Enforcement and lockout recovery.** **Require this connection** on a verified domain removes
  email codes and magic links for its addresses. If the provider is then down or the connection is
  removed, those people can sign in only with a passkey or another link already on their account.
  Recovery is an operator's: **Stop requiring** (step-up), or releasing the domain; the console
  asks for a confirmation that says so. Verification that lapses (the TXT record gone, or 72 hours
  of resolver errors) stops enforcement by itself; a console check that finds the record gone is audited as `domain_unverify`.
- **Delete.** Refused while people sign in through a connection (their links are keyed to its
  issuer) and for the seeded row: turn it off instead.
- **Residual.** An operator with the platform area and a fresh step-up can add a provider whose
  claims a later access rule trusts; that rule names its connection (LX-36), and an unverified
  domain neither routes, vouches nor enforces. The built-in providers (Google, Apple, Steam)
  still read their `SIGNIN_*` Worker values; sealing them in rows is a follow-up.

### Product backends: `X-PKey-License` (SP-53)

An app can send its signed licence document to its developer's own backend, which decides the
request offline with a server drop-in (WIRE-CONTRACT-V4 §14 is the normative form; plans/SP-53.md
the long form). The Worker never reads the header. The rows below are pinned by
`conformance/corpus/v2/backend-matrix.json`, recomputed by an independent reference
(`tools/corpus/reference/backend.ts`) and replayed by client-core and, as they land, every server
core (SP-55 to SP-57, SP-62).

- **Replay (declared, not mitigated).** The document is a bearer credential for its freshness
  window. The device header is a consistency check, not proof of possession, and a backend keeps no
  anti-replay floor, so anyone who captures a document (a proxy log, an APM trace, a shared HAR
  file) can present it from anywhere until it goes stale: `expiresAt + 300` s by default, about 65
  minutes after it was signed, or `maxAgeSeconds + 300` when the backend sets one. Rows
  `ok-replayed-older-document` and `stale-replayed-after-window` pin both edges. TLS, the client's
  refresh rule and header scrubbing keep the exposure short; a device-bound proof is a later
  question (framework drop-ins plan §13 Q3).
- **Revocation bound.** A revoked, expired or disabled licence stops getting documents from the
  Worker, so its last one is refused `license_stale` within the same window (about 65 minutes by
  default). A backend learns of nothing sooner, and the docs say so.
- **Header spoofing.** The document is bound by its signature and its `aud` alone. `X-PKey-Device`
  can only refuse: a value other than the document's `deviceId` is `license_invalid`
  (`invalid-device-mismatch`), so the header cannot re-bind a document to another device. A second
  `X-PKey-License` field, or two documents joined into one value by a proxy, is refused rather than
  picking one (`invalid-two-fields`, `invalid-joined-values`), so a front end and a back end that
  pick differently cannot disagree on whose licence it is. `Authorization`, cookies and query
  parameters are never read (`required-authorization-never-read`), so the credential is not
  ambient and a cross-site request cannot carry it without a CORS preflight the app controls.
- **Backend trust.** The trust set is the pins plus the last manifest verified against the pins
  (§1), per product, chosen by the document's `aud` and re-checked after verification, so one
  product's key never verifies a document for another (`invalid-cross-product-key`), and a
  foreign key under the pinned `kid` fails (`invalid-foreign-key-pinned-kid`). A failed manifest
  fetch keeps the last verified set and the pins always verify, so a Polaris Key outage never
  refuses a document a pinned key signed. A cache of verified documents is keyed by the header's
  SHA-256, dropped when the trust set changes, and never skips the freshness and requirement steps.
- **Fetch amplification.** An unknown `kid` triggers at most one manifest fetch a minute, so junk
  headers cannot be turned into requests to Polaris Key.
- **No secrets in logs.** The header, the JWS and the holder's name and email never appear in a
  log line, an error message or a serialisation; debug logs carry the `kid`, the `aud`, an
  8-character hash of the device id and the refusing step, and the problem body never names the
  step (§14.3). client-core's reference logs nothing.
- **Size and parsing.** The value is capped at 16 384 bytes and must be three base64url segments
  before anything is decoded (`invalid-over-max-bytes`); the strict verifier's own caps,
  duplicate-key refusal and verify-before-parse then apply unchanged.
- **Browser storage.** A web app keeps the document in IndexedDB beside its device token, so an XSS
  that reads one reads both; the docs say so.
- **The client half sends the document only where the app says (SP-58).** `client.backend` refuses
  any origin outside `backend.origins` with `backend-origin-not-allowed`, before anything is sent,
  and names the origin only, never a path or query. A redirect cannot carry the headers elsewhere:
  Node follows redirects itself and checks each hop; `requests` is checked before each hop, the
  retried response included; for `httpx` the per-hop guard (`httpx_client()` or
  `httpx_event_hooks()`) refuses before the hop is sent, and `httpx_auth()` alone is safe only with
  `follow_redirects=False`; the browser fetch never follows a redirect. A backend that answers
  `license_stale` to everything cannot make the client ask the Worker per request: forced syncs
  are at least 10 s apart in every SDK.
- **The native client halves check every hop too (SP-59).** Swift's `data(for:)` refuses a redirect
  to another origin in the task delegate before the hop is sent; Kotlin's network interceptor
  checks each hop and attaches the headers there, because OkHttp keeps custom headers across a
  redirect (an application interceptor alone sends no licence and fails with `not-configured`);
  Godot's `request()` follows redirects by hand and checks each hop, while the raw `headers()` is
  safe only with `max_redirects = 0` (`headers_for(url)` checks the origin).
- **The JWS reaches the Electron renderer (SP-58).** The bridge verb `core.backendHeaders` hands the
  licence document to the renderer, so a compromised renderer holds a bearer credential for the
  freshness window (the replay row above). It never gets the device token or the config document.
  When the host sets `backend.origins`, the verb answers only a request that names one of them
  (`backend-origin-not-allowed` otherwise), so injected script cannot ask for headers for a host
  of its choosing. Without `backend.origins` the verb answers any renderer the bridge already
  trusts; hosts that call a backend should set it.

### One update resolver (P2-12)

The appcast, the channel appcast, `/update/version` and `/release/dl` resolve a release in two
places today: the legacy step reads GitHub on a cache miss, and the store step
(`services/release/resolve.ts`, `storeRelease.ts`) reads the truth store. The first release
adds the store step's inputs, the freshness pass and three migration jobs, and routes nothing to
the store step (`STORE_VIEW_HIDES_ABSENT` is false and no surface is switched). The next release
switches the surfaces once the comparison job's switch rule holds. The rows below are what a
reviewer checks in the first release; the second amends them.

1. **Trust is unchanged.** For a product without release records, whoever can write its GitHub
   releases decides what it serves, as before. A release-level `.sig` is honoured only by the
   legacy renderer, and only after it verifies against `sparkle_ed25519_pub`. The extended
   renderer's rule that only a descriptor's sidecar counts is untouched. The store step adds no
   new writer: its rows are what a sync of the product's own repository wrote, or what a
   described release's descriptor says.
2. **Freshness and deletion.**
   - **The store step makes no GitHub call while serving.** It reads the narrow D1 state and the
     picked row and its artifacts. Resolution therefore stops spending the product's
     `releaseUpstream` budget (4,000 calls an hour) after the switch, and an appcast flood no
     longer reaches the installation quota. The 503 `upstream_rate_limited` answer stays on the
     byte reads that still call GitHub.
   - **A store that is behind serves the newest release it knows**, never one it does not know.
   - **How fresh the store is.** A delivered `release` webhook syncs it at once. Without one,
     the freshness pass (`services/release/freshness.ts`, on the 15-minute connector cron)
     catches up within 15 minutes while the newest release is under 24 hours old, and within 75
     minutes otherwise; the edge adds up to 300 s to either bound. Live reads took up to 90 s
     plus the same 300 s. The cases without a webhook are an asset uploaded, replaced or
     deleted after publication, a missed delivery, and a failed sync.
   - **The pass is bounded and cannot starve.** At most 25 syncs run per tick across all
     products and at most 8 per GitHub App installation (they share one quota); the rest report
     `deferred` and stay due. Within the caps the due product with the oldest `checked_at` goes
     first, never-checked first. A sync that fails or is rate limited writes nothing, so
     `checked_at` stays old and the product stays due; it then backs off for the next 1, 3, 7,
     ... ticks (at most 24, a KV marker that expires), so a repository that always fails cannot
     hold a slot. Its GitHub calls are charged to the product's hourly `releaseUpstream` budget,
     like serving. The pass never throws, and a quota refusal (a thrown
     `UpstreamRateLimitedError` or an answered 429) ends that product's tick. It runs before
     Release's other sweeps, so one that throws does not skip it. A release dated in the future
     does not keep a product due: only the hour rule applies to it.
   - **Edge entries.** Each sync bumps the product's release generation. That drops the KV
     resolution cache at once. It does not purge the edge cache: edge entries live their own
     TTL (120 s or 300 s), which is the 300 s in the bounds above. A sync costs up to 10 list
     calls.
   - **Deletion.** A release is withdrawn once a complete sync sees it gone. A repository with
     more than 1,000 releases never gets a complete read, so nothing is withdrawn there. **A
     yank is the supported way to withdraw a build** and applies at once on every surface.
3. **The classifier and the comparison job (`update.resolver-compare`).** The job is report
   only: it reads and writes nothing in D1, and its `apply` and `down` are delegated to the
   switch rule. It runs both steps on one synthetic request per probe, bypassing the edge cache,
   the access check and the rate limit, so a probe is a diagnostic the lead runs, not a request
   an outsider can make.
   - **Cost and isolation.** The legacy step's resolution cache is private to each product's run
     (an in-memory map in place of KV), so a probe sees GitHub as it is, not a 90-s entry an
     unrelated request left. Everything else, the Sparkle memo included, passes through, so a DMG
     streams at most once per run. Probes are charged to the product's `releaseUpstream` budget.
   - **Pause and checkpoint.** A 403 or 429 from GitHub, or `x-ratelimit-remaining` under 500,
     writes a KV pause marker (expiring, at most an hour, platform-wide, under a key that is not a
     `p:<product>:` key, so no product slug can share it) and the run stops;
     an `UpstreamRateLimitedError` is an `upstream-error` row and pauses that product. A
     checkpoint of the rows done (expiring after an hour) lets the next dry run resume. A lost
     checkpoint only costs a re-run of its probes. The job holds no secret: the rows hold release
     metadata and hashes of response bodies.
   - **The classifier is a pure reading of the store and the two answers.** Six classes are
     expected, because they are the deliberate move to one meaning per track, and two more name
     where the legacy view's floor differed from the live route's; `stale-store` and
     `unexpected` block the switch; `upstream-error` is retried. The one class that widens what a
     caller may see is `beta-includes-stable`: the store's `beta` can answer a stable release the
     legacy `beta` skipped. It is also assigned when the entitlement check refuses the stable
     release the store's `beta` resolved (legacy 404, store 401 or 403), and only after the
     store is asked and does resolve a stable release; a refusal for any other reason stays
     `unexpected`. The widening may only add: where the legacy `beta` answered a release, the
     store's must not be older, so a store that serves an older stable than the legacy
     prerelease is `unexpected`, not `beta-includes-stable`.
   - **Entitlement equivalence is not proved by the dry run.** The probes force public access, so
     the dry run compares what is resolved, not who may have it. That is proved by the golden
     suite (`updateResolverGolden`, `storeSteps`), which runs both steps behind the same grant
     checks. The grant still refuses what it did not cover, so the widening gives a beta caller
     the newest stable release only if their grant allows it.
   - **Two classes absorb by design.** `workflow-channel` and `descriptor-channel` take any
     difference on their selectors, because the two steps mean different things there. The
     checks on them are the switch rule's condition 3 and the golden suite.
   - **The `pr-<n>` lookup.** For a product with a channel workflow, one call lists the last 10
     successful pull-request runs (`actions: read`) and the job probes `pr-<n>` for the pull
     requests they name. The numbers are positive integers from the response, checked, at most
     10, and held in the checkpoint so a resume probes the same list. A refusal leaves the list
     empty.
4. **Least privilege.** The installation token keeps `actions: read` and `pull_requests: read`
   only while a product has a channel workflow. The store step needs neither; a later release
   drops both once the workflow lookups are gone.
5. **The jobs write only what a sync would, and `channel` on undescribed rows.** The lead runs
   them from the console or `pkey migrate`; each is dry-run first, pinned to the report the lead
   read, and audited.
   - **`release.backfill-store`** runs the same sync as the freshness pass for a linked product
     that has no `app` rows or whose listed rows lack `listedAssets`, with its GitHub calls
     charged to the product's `releaseUpstream` budget. Its `down` does nothing: the rows are
     exactly what any sync writes.
   - **`release.materialise-workflow-beta`** sets `release_metadata.channel = 'beta'` on
     undescribed `app` rows whose `channel` is NULL and whose id is in the tag set the product's
     `beta` selector resolves among today. Guards: the apply uses the tag set, workflow and
     branch the dry run recorded and never a fresh read, refuses (`config_changed`) when the
     product's workflow or branch changed since, and sets only ids the dry run listed
     (`wouldSet`). It never marks a release GitHub does not flag as a prerelease that has a semver
     tag: that is a stable build the workflow's set happens to name. The write is one `UPDATE`
     that names the product, the id list, `channel IS NULL` and "undescribed", so a described
     release (its descriptor's `channel` wins), an already channelled row or another product's row
     is never touched. It applies in full or not at all, and `RETURNING` gives exactly the ids it
     set. The change moves those rows into `beta` on the store surfaces (the download page,
     `builds/`, storefront feeds), which is their intended meaning.
   - **`down`** resets exactly the ids the apply returned and the runner stored in its unit
     detail, and only the rows whose `channel` is still `'beta'` and that are still undescribed,
     so a row since described or re-channelled keeps its value. The one remaining window: the
     rows are set between the write and the runner storing that detail. A process killed in that
     gap leaves rows that are `beta`, are in no recorded list and are skipped by a later apply
     (their `channel` is no longer NULL), so `down` cannot reset them. The effect is the
     intended one (the row is a workflow beta). If the audit write fails after the update, the
     apply still returns the ids, with the error in its detail, so `down` keeps its list.
   - **The switch rule.** The second release merges when the latest comparison report has zero
     blocking rows, the lead has acknowledged every expected row by class and count in the
     migration ledger, and no `workflow-channel` row's old answer is a build published after the
     latest materialise run. Until the product's workflow publishes beta as a prerelease or with
     descriptor `channel: beta`, every new short-SHA build would belong to no channel and beta
     and `pr-<n>` testers would silently stop getting builds.

No personal data is added: the reports hold release metadata only.

### SDK API names (SP-35)

A removed trust-pin name is never read. Python's `trust=` (and the `"trust"` key of a generated
config) is gone with no alias: an old call fails with `TypeError` or a missing-pinned-keys
refusal, so an old config cannot set, widen or empty the trust root unnoticed. Godot's
`pinned_trust_keys` follows the same rule: its `_set` keeps a legacy value only to
refuse it and to pre-fill the dock, never as the trust set. A refusal names options, never
values. `conformance/parity/api.json` and its lint are hygiene, not a security boundary.

### The GitHub write path

**What is new.** Polaris Key writes to a customer's repository through the GitHub App: the setup
pull request, the `release` environment and the `v*` tag ruleset. Code:
`services/release/github/{allow,write,prToken}.ts`, `ciFix.ts`.

**Control: a closed allow-list.** Every write is one named action (`setup.branch`, `setup.file`,
`setup.pr`, `env.release`, `ruleset.tags`) with one request shape and one permission set.
`authorize()` in `allow.ts` is the only gate and `write.ts` sends nothing it has not passed; a
request outside the table is refused before any fetch.

**Control: narrowed tokens.** A token is minted per request, for one action's permissions and the
one repository named in the path. It is never cached or stored. The host is fixed to
`api.github.com` and redirects are not followed.

**Control: the never-list.** Refused: merging, closing or retargeting a pull request, deleting a
ref or file, a force update, any branch but `pkey/setup`, the default branch, any path outside
`.pkey/{distribution,release}.{yaml,yml,json}` and `.github/workflows/release.yml`,
collaborators, repository settings, hooks, secrets, and any other repository. A test enforces the
list. Polaris Key opens one pull request; a person merges it.

**Control: the release environment and the tag ruleset.** The environment named `release` is
limited to `v*` tags, and a tag ruleset over `refs/tags/v*` blocks creation, deletion, update and
force push (repository admins bypass), so only an admin can create the release tag a publish job
runs on, and the OIDC token it presents carries `ref_protected: true` only for a protected release
tag. Only the environment the manifest names is written, and only `release`; an existing
environment is never rewritten (a PUT may reset its reviewers), a missing tag policy is added
alone, and CI readiness reports the environment ready only when it lists the `v*` tag policy.
A pull request PATCH and a ruleset PUT are authorized only for the number or id the caller
confirmed in the same operation; an environment write carries no reviewers. The fix route needs a
step-up.

**Open items.**

- The ruleset's bypass actor is the repository-admin role (id 5). GitHub's REST reference does not
  list role ids, so this is unverified on a live repository.

### The CI GitHub token exchange

**What is new.** `POST /<product>/distribution/pr/github-token`
(`services/distribution/pr/githubToken.ts`) gives a CI run a GitHub token to open the pull request
to a declared Homebrew tap or Scoop bucket, so no personal token is stored.

**Control: scope and repository.** The caller is a `pkeyci_` token holding `distribution:pr`, an
opt-in scope (never a default, never a manifest grant). The repository is never the caller's word:
it is the `direct` outlet's declared `homebrewTap` or `scoopBucket`, matched against the
manifest's pattern, which refuses `Homebrew/*` and `ScoopInstaller/*`. Other outlet kinds have no
repository here and are refused. The pattern accepts any owner, so the binding is the
installation: the token is minted only when the installation GitHub reports for the repository is
the product's own linked one (`release_config.gh_installation_id`). A repository of another
customer, and one without the App, answer the same 404, so the route is no oracle for installs.

**Control: the token.** Contents and Pull requests write on that one repository, for GitHub's one
hour. It is in the one response (`Cache-Control: no-store`), not stored, and not audited; the
audit row `distribution.pr.github_token` names the outlet and the repository.

**Control: the rate limit.** 20 requests per product per hour, charged once the body is
well-formed and before any GitHub call. The limiter fails closed, since the route mints a
credential. With Release off the route does not exist.

**Residual.** A `pkeyci_` token with this scope holds Contents write on the declared tap or
bucket for the hour of each token it exchanges. That opens pull requests, and it also allows a
direct push to the default branch and creating branches and tags unless the repository has branch
protection (recommended on every tap and bucket); any later step of the CI job can use it. Anyone who can edit `.pkey/distribution` on the
default branch can change which repository an outlet declares, within the pattern.

### Boundaries that are weaker than they look

- **The SDK cache is inside the attacker's trust domain, and the SDK does not trust it.** Every
  load re-verifies the pin evidence against the pins, the trust manifest against the usable pins
  and each document against the effective set; the decoded document is never stored, and the
  cache supplies no key bytes (R2-01). The client-side rules that close what remained:
  - **The unsigned hints are display state.** A hard 401 deletes the document it answered for,
    and a 403 build block deletes the licence document, in the same write that sets the hint.
    Removing `lastSyncUnauthorized` or `blocked` from the plain-JSON record now yields
    `needs-activation`, not a usable document. Residual: restoring a full pre-revocation snapshot
    of the state directory and token store works until `graceUntil`. A bundle-activated install
    has no token to revoke, so `graceUntil` is its only revocation lever.
  - **Unsigned discovery cannot switch the licence gate off.** The gate is on when the build's
    `expectedServices` (default licence and config) names `license`, or when a discovery loaded
    this session says it is enabled. A config-only product names `expectedServices` without
    `license`.
  - **A copied state directory does not carry the device.** The desktop file store re-derives the
    device id from the hardware anchor at every start and discards a stored id that disagrees,
    with the token and the grant slices of the cache. The probes (`ioreg`, `reg.exe`) run by
    absolute path, not through `PATH`. Keychain and Keystore stores keep their stored id.
    Residual: an attacker who can run code as the user can read the anchor too.
  - **The network path runs on the effective clock** and **every verify call names its
    anti-replay floor**: "no floor" is an explicit `null`.
  - **A bundle activation is a signed fact, not a marker.** The cache keeps the imported bundle's
    own JWS (`bundle`); `activation: "bundle"` needs it to re-verify against the usable pins (no
    import window) with the cached licence document byte-identical to the bundle's, and no token
    held. The old unsigned `importedBundle` marker is not read. An import is refused unless each
    inner document is strictly newer than the cached one of its type, and a held trust manifest
    newer than the bundle's is kept, so an old bundle cannot roll a device back or re-teach a
    revoked key.
  - **A pinned key can be revoked, and the revocation is kept as evidence.** A verified manifest
    signed by one pin that lists another pin's exact bytes as `revoked` tombstones it; the
    manifest itself is stored (`pinRevocations`) and re-verified on every load, in issue order.
    A tombstoned pin verifies nothing again. A manifest revoking its own signer is refused, so an
    install always keeps a usable pin. Residuals: the evidence lives in the user-writable cache, so
    a willing user can delete it (it protects honest installs from a third party holding the key,
    not from the user); and the race is symmetric — whoever holds one pin and reaches a client
    before the operator acts can tombstone the other, which TLS confines to an attacker who can
    also answer for the Worker. With no pin compromised the outcome is never worse than before:
    pins were terminal.
  - **Key statuses and base64url are strict.** Only `active`, `staged` and `retired` keep a
    published key (a missing or unknown status skips it); every JWS segment and trust-set key must
    be canonical base64url, so a lenient decoder's spare spellings of a signature or key are
    refused everywhere.
- **A linked GitHub repo is a control-plane input, not just a data source.** `.pkey/` manifests
  rewrite tiers, OIDC issuer, artifact policy, and admin group on resync. Edge-mint recipes are
  the exception that is held back: a recipe from `.pkey/` is **inert until an operator approves
  it** in the exact form it will run (`edge_mint_approvals`), and any push that changes a
  security-relevant field makes it inert again. A repo writer can name a secret in a recipe but
  cannot make that secret signable, nor make an unapproved recipe mint. An approval is also bound
  to the three product settings that decide who can hold a device token the mint accepts, because
  a push can change each of them without touching the recipe. (a) Whether the mint is public: the
  open-registration acknowledgement is stored on the approval, so a push that makes the mint
  public — turning License and Identity off so the derived policy is open (the policy cannot be
  declared: `devices.registration` is removed), enabling anonymous `autoIssue` enrolment (which
  hands any caller a licence and a device
  token while registration still reads `requires-license`), or turning on an OIDC default tier
  with Identity on (every account the IdP signs in gets a licence) — widens an approval given
  without it. (b) Whether licences are checked: the mint requires a usable licence only while
  License is on, and with Identity on a push that turns License off keeps the mint closed
  (`requires-identity`) while letting a device whose licence was disabled or expired mint again;
  the approval records whether License was on, the approve call echoes it (`409` if it changed
  since the console loaded), and the console warns while License is off, so a re-approval after
  a License-off push cannot record "no licence checks" unseen. (c) The sign-in trust: on a closed product, signing
  in is the other route to a device token, and the manifest writes the OIDC provider, issuer,
  client id and `groupRoleMap` that decide who a sign-in licenses. The approval records them (and
  whether Identity was on); while Identity is on, any change widens it. A widened approval stops
  matching at once (every mint re-checks), **and it is deleted before anything can revert the
  widening**: every writer of an approval input sweeps the approvals the product has ALREADY
  widened before it writes — resync before its first write, and the console before every write of
  `services_json` or `auto_issue_json` (the services and License-policy PATCH and revert) — and
  audits each drop as `config.mint.invalidate`. The guarantee rests on that pre-write sweep. Resync
  also sweeps after its last write, in a `finally`, so a push that throws half-way (say, a
  duplicated recipe id) is caught at once; but a `finally` does not run when the Worker is killed
  after the push's un-batched writes (a CPU-heavy manual-channel regex, a cancelled webhook), nor
  does it see an approve that races it — the next push or console edit drops those before it
  writes. So a push that aims sign-in at an issuer the pusher controls, opens
  enrolment or turns License off, followed by a push that reverts it, leaves the recipe `pending`
  rather than approved; it mints again only when an operator re-approves it. Recipe-field changes
  are not swept (a changed recipe signs nothing meanwhile), so reverting one restores the
  approval. The upgrade backfill records the acknowledgement only for recipes that were already
  public mints at deploy, and the License and sign-in state as deployed. **Residuals:** (1) the
  licences and device tokens issued while an approval was widened survive a re-approval — the
  ingest drops the approval, not what was handed out meanwhile — so before re-approving, an
  operator reviews the audit log from the `config.mint.invalidate` row on and disables what they
  did not intend; (2) an approval trusts the identity provider itself — anyone that IdP signs in
  with a mapped group (including accounts its administrator adds later) is covered, which is the
  IdP weakness below, not something the approval can close; (3) a widening that no sweep has seen
  yet (an operator's own console edit, or a push killed before its post-write sweep) lasts until
  the next push or console edit drops the approval — the per-mint check refuses while it lasts,
  but anonymous enrolments or sign-ins it allows in the meantime are issued, and fall under (1).
- **A minted token carries its recipe on its catalog entry (U-31).** The recipe is the entry's
  `mint` block, from `.pkey/schema` or from a console catalog publish, so there is one place to
  author it and the same approval gates both: the block is lifted out of the catalog into
  `edge_mint_config` (the public `/schema` document never carries a signing-secret name or a claims
  template), and a recipe nobody has approved as it stands answers `404` exactly as before. The
  block is held to the manifest's own rules (alg, secret-name alphabet, one-hour ceiling, `requires`,
  key = recipe id), a block and a legacy `edgeMint[]` recipe of one id are refused, and a console
  publish writes the recipe inside the catalog's claim guard, so a lost claim or refused publish saves
  nothing. A console save is **not** an approval: it leaves the approval row alone, so a changed
  recipe goes `changed` and signs nothing, and an unchanged one keeps its approval. Approving is the
  one new gate: `POST …/config/mint/<id>/approve` needs a step-up (a sign-in from the last five
  minutes), so a stolen or idle console session cannot approve a recipe an attacker just saved.
  The console owns the recipes it saved: with `config.catalog` claimed, a resync neither deletes nor
  rewrites them (SQL-guarded against a claim that lands mid-resync), and dropping or un-minting an
  entry removes its recipe and approval in the same batch. An entry published without a block leaves
  its recipe untouched, since the served catalog never carries one. **Residual:** an operator who
  can publish the catalog can point a recipe at any `edge-mint`-usage secret; the approval, which
  shows the signing secret and who may mint, is what stands between that and a mint.
- **Which commit's `.pkey/` is applied, and the record of it (R6-05, ST-01a).** A push to ANY
  branch touching `.pkey/` triggers a resync, but the push only triggers it: `resyncRepo` and
  `linkRepo` ask GitHub for the DB-configured repository's default-branch head
  (`GET /repos/{o}/{r}/commits/HEAD`, `Accept: application/vnd.github.sha`) and read every
  document `?ref=<that sha>` (`services/release/manifestFetch.ts`). The ref is a value GitHub
  just returned for the repository's own default branch, never the webhook's `after` nor anything
  in a request, so branch protection and required review on `.pkey/` still bound what is applied;
  pinning also removes the window in which a push landing between two Contents reads mixed
  documents from two commits. A failed or malformed head answer fails the apply closed, with no
  unpinned fallback. The webhook's `after` is still stored, as `product_sync_state.commit_sha`,
  and shown only as "Triggered by push". Every apply (link, resync, and the system product's
  deploy hook, which records the deploy's own `PKEY_GIT_SHA`) writes one
  `product_manifest_snapshot` row in the apply's batch: the applied commit, a SHA-256 over the raw
  documents and the parsed manifest. Manifests name secrets but never carry values, so the row
  holds no secret material; it is latest-only and, like every product-scoped table, references
  the product without `ON DELETE` (R11-01). The snapshot
  records what was applied and never decides it. **Residual:** the backfill (ST-01c) may fetch at
  the webhook-supplied `commit_sha` to corroborate an old row; that read is compare-only, never
  applied, and the row it writes says so.
- **Resync as a write path, and console claims (ST-01b, notes/S-18 §4.5).** A repo push changes
  product settings: the name, the licence defaults (which set `graceUntil` and the activation
  seat count), the web origins (the CORS allow-list), the admin group, the catalog, tiers and
  profiles. Three controls bound it. (1) **Visibility**: every setting or tier/profile row a resync
  changes gets its own `setting.resync` audit row (before → after) in the apply's batch, so a
  silent revert of a console edit is no longer possible and a hostile push is attributable to the
  applied commit. (2) **Claims**: a console write to a claimable setting (`core.name`,
  `license.defaults.*`, `core.web.origins`, `config.catalog`) upserts a `source = 'console'` row in
  `product_settings`, and a console create or edit of a tier or profile marks that row `console`;
  every later resync skips them. The guard is in each write statement, not only in the resync's
  early read of the claims: the five column writes keep the column while a live `product_settings`
  claim exists (`CASE WHEN EXISTS …`), the catalog deactivate/insert and their audit rows carry
  `NOT EXISTS`, and tiers and profiles carry `WHERE source = 'manifest'`, so a console edit that
  claims a key while a push is between its GitHub reads and its batch is never overwritten.
  Revert deletes the claim and re-applies the last snapshot (ST-01a), audited as
  `setting.revert`; a reverted catalog is screened with `compileAll()` first (409
  `invalid_catalog`, claim kept), because a resync does not screen a claimed catalog yet still
  records it in the snapshot, so Revert would otherwise be an unscreened path to `product_schema`
  and to unbounded `pattern` complexity. `core.adminGroup` is manifest-only: the console refuses it on a linked
  product rather than storing a value the next push would silently replace. (3) **No half-applied
  refusal**: every check (OIDC issuer, publisher lookup, catalog compile, binary name, the
  referenced-tier and referenced-profile guards) runs before the first write and the apply is ONE
  `db.batch`, so a refused or throwing push writes nothing — including the `services_json` and
  `auto_issue_json` widenings P0-12's post-write sweep used to clean up after. A push still
  deletes a manifest-sourced tier or profile it dropped when nothing references it, and never a
  console row; a console row holding a new manifest id is kept and reported as a conflict.
  **Residual:** claims make the console the stronger writer for those keys, so a stolen admin
  session (T7) can now pin a value that the repo cannot override until someone reverts it; the
  claim, its author and the revert are all audited, and a manifest-authoritative product (below)
  takes only expiring, reason-bearing break-glass claims. Existing rows default to `manifest`
  until ST-01c's backfill runs.
- **Manifest-authoritative mode and break-glass claims (ST-20, notes/S-18 §4.5 items 7–8).** A
  product setting, `core.manifest.authoritative`, makes `.pkey/` the only writer of its claimable
  settings: the one write path, `writeSetting()` (ST-04), refuses a console write to them (409
  `manifest_authoritative`) unless it carries `breakGlass: { reason }` (1–500 characters; L2 in the
  console), and that claim's `product_settings.expires_at` is at most 7 days out (a shorter
  `breakGlass.seconds` may be asked for, never a longer one). The products PATCH, the catalog
  publish and the row-backed settings' `PATCH …/settings/<key>` all write through it. An apply ends it
  sooner, in the apply's own batch, when the manifest it applies declares a different value for the
  field than the last applied snapshot did (`claimsForApply`), so committing the fix to `.pkey/`
  takes the field back; an apply that leaves the field alone keeps the claim, so an unrelated push or
  deploy cannot undo an incident fix. An expired claim stops counting at once (every claim guard
  reads `expires_at > now`, no job needed) and its row is removed, audited, at the next apply. The
  ending is guarded twice: the row is deleted only at the version read (a re-claim made since
  survives), and the value write and the `setting.breakGlass.end` audit row run only while no live
  claim remains. Off by default for a customer product (an operator writes it, audited; only a
  repo-linked product may turn it on). **The system product** is manifest-authoritative by a
  registry rule, not a row: `systemLock` on the entry, which the registry test requires for every
  key `SYSTEM_LOCKED_KEYS` names, so no console write or deleted row turns it off (409 `locked`).
  Its single writer is the deploy hook (§3 "The deploy hook"): a GitHub webhook push to the monorepo,
  the console's Resync and its dry run are refused ("the system product is applied by the deploy
  hook", reason `system_product`) before any GitHub read and without a sync-state row, so the
  manifest applied to it is always the deployed tag's, never the default branch's head. Every resync
  answer, the console's result panel, `product_sync_state`'s message, the deploy hook's answer and its
  platform activity row list the live break-glass claims. **Residual:** a stolen admin session (T7)
  can still make a break-glass claim, but it needs a reason that is audited, it ends within 7 days
  or at the next apply that changes the field, and every deploy names it in the job log (as a
  warning). The deploy job's log may be readable beyond the operators, so the hook's answer carries
  each claim's key and expiry only; the reason and the claimant stay in the console and the
  platform activity row. The mode governs every claimable setting claimed through a
  `product_settings` row: the five column-backed claim keys and LX-06's row-backed keys (below).
  The settings still claimed through their older markers (`services_source`, `compat_source`,
  `access_source`, the fingerprint and auto-issue policies) and the rich ones (tier and profile
  rows, the trusted publisher) are not yet refused by it: their markers are the deploy hook's to
  honour, and ST-05 decides them with the generic API.
- **Row-backed claimable settings (LX-06, `core/rowSettings.ts`).** The licensing settings
  (`licensing.*`) and `identity.oidc.syncTierOnSignIn` keep their VALUE in the `product_settings`
  row (`value_json`): no row means the registry default, `source = 'manifest'` the last applied
  `.pkey/` value, `source = 'console'` a claim. A push writes them through License's and
  Identity's `manifestIngestAlways` with the same in-statement claim guard as above (the upsert
  and its `setting.resync` audit row are `WHERE NOT EXISTS` a live console row), so a claim made
  mid-resync still wins; a setting the manifest stops declaring loses its manifest row and returns
  to the default (omit-clears, S-18 §4.5 item 1), never a console row. The console writes them
  through `GET …/settings/effective`, `PATCH` and `DELETE …/settings/<key>`: platform admin
  session and CSRF like every admin write; the value is checked against the registry entry
  server-side; a critical key needs a reason, enforced by the Worker, not the console; every
  write carries a required `expectedVersion`, compared before the write and again in the write's
  own `WHERE`; and the write goes through `writeSetting()` (ST-04), whose audit row and claim
  apply all-or-nothing, so the loser of a race gets a 409 and leaves no row claiming it wrote. A
  manifest-authoritative product (the system product always) takes a console write only as a
  break-glass claim (above); Revert stays open. `upgradeOnly`
  for `identity.oidc.syncTierOnSignIn` would let an identity provider's groups raise a licence's
  tier, so the registry marks it security-widening (critical, at least L1 to widen, never
  inherited from platform). Nothing reads it yet: the behaviour behind it, and the licensing
  model's own threats (T1–T10), are LX-22's to add here when they ship.
- **The IdP is trusted for `groups`, and `groups` is the entire admin authorization decision.**

## 4. Adversaries

| ID  | Adversary                                                                                               | Capability                                                                           | Motivation                                                                                                                                                                                        | Priority                           |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| T1  | **Unauthenticated internet attacker**                                                                   | HTTP to `key.plrs.im`, can read public discovery/JWKS, can register nothing          | Control-plane takeover                                                                                                                                                                            | **Highest**                        |
| T2  | **Release-channel attacker**                                                                            | Holds the webhook secret, or write access to a linked repo, or GitHub App compromise | Ship code to end users                                                                                                                                                                            | **Highest**                        |
